entries.question: Avery attacks with a [Guile] that was turned face-down by [Ixidron], and Nelson blocks with [Jerrard of the Closed Fist]. Does Avery shuffle?
entries.reason: Both conclude that Guile is destroyed, is in the graveyard with its "put into a graveyard from anywhere" trigger, and that trigger causes Avery to shuffle it into their library.
entries.answer:
Yes — Avery shuffles Guile into their library.

Why: while it's on the battlefield turned face down by Ixidron, Guile is a 2/2 with no name, no text, and no abilities [708.2b, Ixidron ruling #4]. That means (a) it does not have "can't be blocked except by three or more creatures," so Nelson's single blocker Jerrard of the Closed Fist is a legal block, and (b) Jerrard of the Closed Fist's 6 power is lethal to the 2/2, so the face-down Guile is destroyed in the combat damage step.

Once it's put into the graveyard, it is no longer a face-down permanent — in the graveyard it's just the card Guile with all its normal characteristics and abilities. Guile's last ability, "When Guile is put into a graveyard from anywhere, shuffle it into its owner's library," is not a leaves-the-battlefield ability; it triggers from the graveyard [Guile ruling #5, Guile ruling #0]. So the trigger goes on the stack and, on resolution, Guile is shuffled into Avery's library. (Contrast the Yixlid Jailer case, where the ability is missing *in the graveyard* — then it wouldn't trigger [Guile ruling #7].)

Even if someone removes Guile from the graveyard in response to the trigger, Avery still shuffles their library; Guile just stays in its new zone [701.24c, Guile ruling #2].

Also note Ixidron's power/toughness is defined by the number of face-down creatures on the battlefield, so it shrinks by 1 after the face-down Guile dies.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same at a two-player or multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Yes. By default, triggered abilities are checked immediately after the event in question to see if they should trigger. At that point, the Guile is face-up in the graveyard and has that ability.

(Guile's trigger does not fit the exception for "leaves-the-battlefield" triggers because it is a "from anywhere" trigger.)

entries.question: Archer attacks with a [The Scarab God] that was turned face-down by [Ixidron] and Nia blocks with [Scathe Zombies]. Does The Scarab God trigger?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude no trigger because the Scarab God is face down due to Ixidron and has no abilities at the moment blockers are declared, so nothing triggers.
entries.answer:
No. While The Scarab God is face down due to Ixidron, it has no abilities at all, so nothing about it triggers when Nia blocks with Scathe Zombies — and in any case The Scarab God has no "becomes blocked" ability to begin with.

Why: creatures turned face down by Ixidron are 2/2 creatures with no text, no name, no subtypes, and no mana cost [Ixidron ruling #4]. "No text" means the face-down The Scarab God has lost its upkeep trigger, its {2}{U}{B} activated ability, and its "When The Scarab God dies, return it to its owner's hand" trigger. So during the declare blockers step, when Scathe Zombies is declared as a blocker and the abilities that trigger on blockers being declared would trigger [509.1i], there is nothing on the face-down The Scarab God to trigger [509.3, 509.3c].

Two consequences worth noting:
- If the face-down The Scarab God dies in combat (for example, trading with a larger blocker), the death trigger does not go on the stack, because the permanent had no text when it died. It just goes to the graveyard, where it is again a face-up The Scarab God card.
- If The Scarab God were somehow turned face up before blockers were declared, it would have its abilities again, but it still has no ability that triggers on becoming blocked, so nothing would trigger from Nia's block anyway.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming The Scarab God is still face down at the moment blockers are declared. A trigger condition must actually be met at that moment by an ability that exists then [603.2f], and abilities keyed to blockers being declared check the game state at that point [509.3c, 509.3f] — so if it were turned face up only after blockers were declared, that would not retroactively create any trigger either.

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more; nothing here depends on the number of opponents (The Scarab God's upkeep ability that affects "each opponent" is not functioning while it's face down).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. By default, triggered abilities are checked immediately after the event in question to see if they should trigger. However, "leaves-the-battlefield" triggers check the game state immediately before the event instead. At that point, The Scarab God had no abilities.

entries.question: Alaia casts [Biogenic Upgrade] targeting [Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11]. In total how many counters are be placed on Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11?
entries.reason: Both conclude nine +1/+1 counters are placed, correctly applying Michelangelo’s replacement effect to the initial three (making four) and again to the doubled placement (adding five) for a total of nine.
entries.answer:
Nine +1/+1 counters total are placed on Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11, leaving it with nine counters (a 10/10).

How it works:

1. Distribution step: with only one target, all three counters from Biogenic Upgrade must go to Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 (each target must get at least one — [Biogenic Upgrade ruling #0]). Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's own static ability says if one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on a creature you control, that many plus one are put on it instead, so 3 becomes 4. Card text like this overrides the default counter placement. Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 now has 4 counters.

2. Doubling step: doubling means putting a number of +1/+1 counters on it equal to the number it already has ([701.10e], [Biogenic Upgrade ruling #2]), i.e. 4 more. Because that placement is again "one or more +1/+1 counters put on a creature you control," Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's ability adds one, so 5 are put on. Other effects that care about counters being put on it interact with the doubling normally ([Biogenic Upgrade ruling #2]).

Total placed: 4 + 5 = 9 counters. Each +1/+1 counter adds +1/+1 in layer 7c ([122.1a], [613.4c]), so the 1/1 Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 becomes 10/10.

Assumption on timing/targets: I assume Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 is the only target and had no +1/+1 counters beforehand. If it already had N counters, the doubling would put N+4 counters (plus one) on it instead; and if Alaia split the three counters among multiple creatures, Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 would only get its assigned share plus one before doubling.

Player count doesn't matter here — the result is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game, since Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 is Alaia's own creature.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Nine. Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's ability is a replacement effect that applies whenever counters are being placed on it When Biogenic Upgrade begins resolving, that replacement effect will add a counter, resulting in Alaia placing four +1/+1 counters. Afterwards, Biogenic Upgrade will then double the amount of counters on Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11. This results in an additional four counters being placed on it, which will then be modified by Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's replacement effect again, resulting in nine +1/+1 counters in total.

entries.question: Addison casts [Ferocious Zheng]. After it resolves, they cast [Elemental Eruption] and reveal [Everdream] from their hand, splicing it onto Elemental Eruption. When Elemental Eruption's Storm trigger resolves, will the copies of Elemental Eruption also have Everdream spliced onto them?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that storm copies inherit the splice choice, so each copy of Elemental Eruption will have Everdream spliced onto it.
entries.answer:
Yes. Each copy created by Elemental Eruption's storm ability will have Everdream's text spliced onto it, so each copy both creates a 4/4 red Dragon Elemental token with flying and prowess and then draws Addison a card.

Why: splicing is a choice made while casting Elemental Eruption (Everdream is revealed from hand and its splice cost {2}{U} paid as part of casting), and copying a spell copies its characteristics and all decisions made for it [707.10]. Everdream's own ruling states this directly: if a spell is copied, the copy will have the same abilities spliced onto it as the original [Everdream ruling #4]. The spliced text becomes part of Elemental Eruption's rules text as a text-changing effect [702.47c], [612.10], and Everdream's effect happens after Elemental Eruption's own effect [702.47b], [Everdream ruling #1]. Note also that text referring to a card by name in spliced text refers to the spell on the stack, not the Everdream card [702.47c].

Count of copies: storm copies the spell once for each other spell cast before it this turn [702.40a]. Since Ferocious Zheng was the only earlier spell, Addison gets one copy — total of two token-creating, card-drawing resolutions (the copy plus Elemental Eruption itself).

The copy is put directly onto the stack and isn't cast, so it won't be counted by a later storm spell this turn [Elemental Eruption ruling #2], and it also isn't a new casting that would let Addison splice additional cards onto it. Copies can be countered individually; countering Elemental Eruption itself doesn't remove the copies [Elemental Eruption ruling #0]. If Elemental Eruption were countered, the spliced Everdream card would just stay in hand [Everdream ruling #0] — but that's moot here since the splice cost was already paid and, if countered, the splice changes are lost when the spell leaves the stack [702.47e].

None of this depends on player count: the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, except that storm counts spells cast by all players earlier in the turn, so with more players there may be more prior spells and thus more copies.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. As Addison is casting Elemental Eruption they choose whether they want to splice as part of the casting process. When the storm trigger resolves it copies all the choices made when casting the original spell, including the choice to splice.

entries.question: Nova controls a [Torsten Von Ursus] enchanted by their [Felidar Umbra]. Allen activates the last ability of [Sorin, Lord of Innistrad], targeting the Torsten Von Ursus. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate agrees the Umbra is destroyed and Torsten survives but contradicts the reference by saying Allen gets nothing (and leaving the return-to-battlefield unresolved) instead of stating the Umbra is returned to the battlefield under Allen's control and reattaches to Torsten.
entries.answer:
Torsten Von Ursus survives. Because Nova's Felidar Umbra grants umbra armor ("If enchanted permanent would be destroyed, instead remove all damage marked on it and destroy this Aura"), the "destroy" part of Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's −6 ability is replaced for Torsten Von Ursus: all damage marked on Torsten Von Ursus is removed, Torsten Von Ursus is not destroyed and stays on the battlefield under Nova's control, and Felidar Umbra is destroyed instead and put into Nova's graveyard [702.89a]. This replacement is mandatory, not optional [Felidar Umbra ruling #3], and it applies no matter why the creature would be destroyed — including a plain "destroy" effect like Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's [Felidar Umbra ruling #5].

Since Torsten Von Ursus was never put into a graveyard, the "Return each card put into a graveyard this way to the battlefield under your control" clause finds no Torsten Von Ursus card to steal — Allen gets nothing from that target. It is also not regeneration: Torsten Von Ursus does not become tapped and is not removed from combat, and "can't be regenerated" wording wouldn't stop it [Felidar Umbra ruling #6].

One subtlety: per [Felidar Umbra ruling #7], when a spell or ability says it would "destroy" the enchanted creature, that spell or ability is what destroys the Aura — umbra armor merely changes its effect. So Felidar Umbra is a card destroyed by Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's ability, which raises the question of whether Allen's ability returns Felidar Umbra to the battlefield under Allen's control. The rules provided here don't include the rules on Auras entering the battlefield or on what "put into a graveyard this way" covers for replaced destruction, so I can't settle that sub-point from this context; the main outcome (Torsten Von Ursus lives, damage removed, Felidar Umbra destroyed) is certain.

If Torsten Von Ursus somehow had indestructible, umbra armor would do nothing at all and Felidar Umbra would stay attached [Felidar Umbra ruling #9]. If Nova had a second umbra armor Aura on Torsten Von Ursus, only one Aura would be destroyed, and Nova chooses which [Felidar Umbra ruling #2]. Nothing here depends on player count, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table; Allen simply chooses which creatures to target.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The Felidar Umbra is destroyed instead of the Torsten Von Ursus. It is then returned to the battlefield by the rest of Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's ability. The only creature on the battlefield is the Torsten Von Ursus, so the Felidar Umbra must enter the battlefield enchanting the Torsten Von Ursus. Felidar Umbra is now controlled by Allen.

entries.question: Nico controls [Containment Priest]. Alma attempts to play [Dryad Arbor], which is exiled. Can Alma now play [Sequestered Stash] as their land for turn?
entries.reason: Both conclude that playing Dryad Arbor counts as Alma's one land play (even though it's exiled by Containment Priest), so she cannot also play Sequestered Stash this turn absent an extra land play or an effect that puts it onto the battlefield.
entries.answer:
No. Alma has already used their one land play for the turn on Dryad Arbor, so Alma can't play Sequestered Stash this turn (absent an effect granting an additional land play).

Why: Playing a land is a special action that doesn't use the stack — the land simply goes onto the battlefield and is never a spell [305.1] [701.18a]. Dryad Arbor is both a land and a creature, so it can only be played as a land, not cast [305.9] [300.2a] [Dryad Arbor ruling #4]. Because it was played and not cast, Nico's Containment Priest sees a nontoken creature entering that wasn't cast and exiles it instead [Containment Priest ruling #1].

That exile doesn't refund anything. The land play was still made: to see whether another land can be played, you compare how many lands Alma may play this turn to how many Alma has already played this turn, and playing Dryad Arbor counts as one played land [305.2a] [305.2b] [Dryad Arbor ruling #4]. Since the count is now equal, Alma can't play Sequestered Stash, and any instruction telling Alma to do so is ignored [305.2b] [101.2].

Alma could play Sequestered Stash only if some continuous effect increases Alma's land plays this turn, or if a spell/ability *puts* it onto the battlefield, which isn't "playing a land" and doesn't use a land play [305.4].

This works the same regardless of the number of players at the table; nothing here depends on how many opponents there are. Note also that if Alma had somehow been able to play Dryad Arbor on someone else's turn, that would be illegal anyway [305.3] [Dryad Arbor ruling #6].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Regardless of what zone Dryad Arbor moved to, it was still played as Alma's land play, and Alma can only play one land each turn.

entries.question: Norah controls [Blood Sun]. Ari plays [Dark Depths] and then destroys the Blood Sun with [Sultai Charm]. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference — Dark Depths enters with no ice counters under Blood Sun and, when Blood Sun is destroyed, its “no ice counters” trigger fires and creates the Marit Lage token.
entries.answer:
Ari gets Marit Lage — a 20/20 black legendary Avatar creature token with flying and indestructible.

Step by step:

1. While Norah's Blood Sun is on the battlefield, "All lands lose all abilities except mana abilities." Dark Depths is a land, so as soon as it's on the battlefield it has none of its abilities. Critically, its "enters with ten ice counters on it" ability is an ability that modifies how it enters the battlefield, and Blood Sun strips that ability before it can apply [Blood Sun ruling #5]. So Dark Depths enters the battlefield with zero ice counters. Its {3} counter-removal ability and its last triggered ability are also gone (note that Dark Depths has no mana ability at all, so nothing of it survives Blood Sun) [Dark Depths ruling #0].

2. Ari casts Sultai Charm choosing the mode "Destroy target artifact or enchantment," targeting Blood Sun. Blood Sun is an enchantment, so that's a legal target, and it's destroyed.

3. The moment Blood Sun leaves the battlefield, Dark Depths immediately regains all of its abilities. Its last ability, "When Dark Depths has no ice counters on it, sacrifice it. If you do, create Marit Lage...", is a state trigger [Dark Depths ruling #1]. Dark Depths currently has no ice counters, so the condition is already true and the ability triggers right away — it will be put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority, before anyone acts [117.2d].

4. When that triggered ability resolves, Ari sacrifices Dark Depths and creates the Marit Lage token. (If Dark Depths somehow left the battlefield first, Ari couldn't sacrifice it and would get no token [Dark Depths ruling #2]; and if the trigger were countered while Dark Depths remained on the battlefield with no ice counters, it would simply trigger again [Dark Depths ruling #1].)

Assumption on timing: I'm reading it as Dark Depths entering while Blood Sun was already on the battlefield, then Blood Sun being destroyed afterward — that's what makes the combo work. If instead Dark Depths had entered before Blood Sun existed, it would already have ten ice counters on it, and destroying Blood Sun would just give it its abilities back with those ten counters still there — no free Marit Lage.

Player count doesn't change anything here: this interaction is purely between Dark Depths, Blood Sun, and Sultai Charm, so it works identically in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Dark Depths entered the battlefield with no ice counters, since it didn't have the ability that would cause it to enter with them. When Blood Sun is destroyed, Dark Depths triggers since it has no ice counters on it and creates a Marit Lage token.

entries.question: Aiden controls [Volrath's Shapeshifter] and [Yixlid Jailer]. The top card of their graveyard is [Mistform Skyreaver]. Does Volrath's Shapeshifter have flying?
entries.reason: Both conclude Volrath's Shapeshifter gains the Mistform Skyreaver's full text (including flying) on the battlefield and Yixlid Jailer only removes abilities from the card while it's in the graveyard, so Volrath still has flying.
entries.answer:
Yes — Volrath's Shapeshifter has flying (and is a 6/6 blue Illusion named Mistform Skyreaver with the {1}: type-changing ability, plus its own "{2}: Discard a card.").

Why: Volrath's Shapeshifter's ability is a text-changing effect, not a copy effect [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #5]. It says the permanent has the "full text" of the creature card on top of your graveyard, which sets its name, mana cost, color, types, abilities, power, and toughness [612.6], and it keeps its granted "{2}: Discard a card." ability on top of what it gains [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #1].

Yixlid Jailer says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities." That effect removes abilities from the Mistform Skyreaver card while it sits in Aiden's graveyard; it does not rewrite that card's text, and it does not apply to Volrath's Shapeshifter, which is on the battlefield, not in a graveyard. Because Volrath's Shapeshifter takes the full text of Mistform Skyreaver rather than "copying the abilities it currently has," the flying and the {1} ability appear in Volrath's Shapeshifter's own text on the battlefield, where Yixlid Jailer has no reach. Note also that Yixlid Jailer's own rulings show its ability-removal is limited to the graveyard object and doesn't stop text/characteristic-defining results from applying elsewhere (e.g., changeling still grants all creature types in the graveyard [Yixlid Jailer ruling #1], and "as it enters" abilities still apply when the card leaves the graveyard for the battlefield [Yixlid Jailer ruling #3]).

Practical effect: Volrath's Shapeshifter with flying can't be blocked except by creatures with flying and/or reach, and it can block creatures with or without flying [702.9b]. Multiple instances of flying would be redundant [702.9c]. Nothing here depends on player count, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

One caveat on timing: this holds continuously while Mistform Skyreaver is the top card of the graveyard; if a different card (or a noncreature card) becomes the top card, Volrath's Shapeshifter reverts to a 0/1 blue creature with only "{2}: Discard a card." [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #0], and that change doesn't trigger any "enters" abilities [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #4], [707.4].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Yixlid Jailer only removes abilities, not text, and text is what Volrath's Shapeshifter cares about. Volrath's Shapeshifter also gains the text of the Mistform Skyreaver before Yixlid Jailer removes the abilities.

entries.question: Autumn controls [Bridge from Below] and [Silvercoat Lion]. They cast [Hour of Revelation]. Do they create a Zombie token?
entries.reason: Both conclude no Zombie is created because Bridge from Below was on the battlefield immediately before Hour of Revelation destroyed the creatures, so its graveyard-based trigger does not trigger.
entries.answer:
No — Autumn does not get a Zombie token.

Bridge from Below only functions while it is in a graveyard; while it's on the battlefield it does nothing at all [Bridge from Below ruling #1]. When Hour of Revelation resolves, it destroys all nonland permanents, so Bridge from Below and Silvercoat Lion are put into Autumn's graveyard simultaneously. Bridge from Below's first ability is a look-back-in-time trigger: the game checks the state immediately before the event to see whether the ability existed and whether its condition was met [603.10a]. Immediately before Silvercoat Lion died, Bridge from Below was still on the battlefield, not in the graveyard, so the ability wasn't there to trigger — and per its own ruling, if Bridge from Below isn't in your graveyard immediately before a creature dies, its abilities don't trigger at all [Bridge from Below ruling #0]. No token is created [701.7a].

For completeness on the cost: Hour of Revelation costs {3}{W}{W}{W}, and only the generic {3} is reduced (to nothing) if there are ten or more nonland permanents on the battlefield when you cast it, leaving {W}{W}{W}; the three white symbols are never reduced. Cost is locked in when you cast it, before payment [Hour of Revelation ruling #0].

This answer doesn't depend on player count: it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since Bridge from Below cares only about which graveyard the creature went to, not who controlled it [Bridge from Below ruling #3]. If instead Bridge from Below had already been in Autumn's graveyard when Hour of Revelation destroyed Silvercoat Lion, the trigger would happen and Autumn would create a 2/2 black Zombie — provided Bridge from Below is still in the graveyard as that ability resolves [Bridge from Below ruling #0].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Leaves-the-battlefield triggers care about the state of the game immediately before the event in question. Bridge from Below was on the battlefield at that time, and won't trigger.

entries.question: Axl activates [Ring of Ma'rûf]'s ability in their upkeep. What happens in Axl's draw step if they don't own any cards outside the game?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Ring of Ma'rûf's replacement effect replaces Axl's draw with putting a card they own from outside the game into their hand, and if they own none then the draw is replaced with nothing.
entries.answer:
Axl's draw-step draw is replaced and Axl ends up with no card: the Ring of Ma'rûf ability says "The next time you would draw a card this turn, instead put a card you own from outside the game into your hand," so the turn-based draw at the start of the draw step (rule 504.1) never happens, and because Axl owns no cards outside the game there is nothing to put into hand. Net effect: Axl skips their draw for the turn entirely and gains nothing.

Why: "Outside the game" means cards not in any of the game's zones — sideboard/collection cards, not a zone at all (400.11c). Ring of Ma'rûf is a replacement effect, not a "you may" choice, and a draw-replacement effect is applied even when the replacement can't actually produce anything (121.6a, 614.11). The Ring of Ma'rûf ruling makes the point explicitly: it replaces your next draw rather than simply putting a card into your hand.

Two side notes:
- Since no draw actually occurs, Axl is not "attempting to draw from an empty library," so the loss-the-game state-based action (121.4, 704.5b) is not triggered even if Axl's library were empty.
- I'm assuming Axl activated it during the beginning phase of their own turn before the draw step, so the draw step's turn-based draw is the "next time you would draw." If some earlier draw had already occurred that turn (for example from another effect resolving first), that earlier draw would have been the one replaced and the draw step draw would proceed normally.

This works the same regardless of the number of players; nothing here depends on the player count.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Axl is required to attempt to find a card from outside the game, if they fail to find one, then when the ability resolves they will put nothing into their hand. Since Ring of Ma'rûf sets up a replacement effect, Axl can't choose to ignore it.

entries.question: Athena control [Krark, the Thumbless] and [Spark Double] copying it. They cast [Song of Totentanz], which triggers both Krark, the Thumbless. When the first trigger resolves they lose the flip and return Song of Totentanz to hand. What happens when the second trigger resolves?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference: a lost second flip does nothing and a won second flip creates a copy of Song of Totentanz.
entries.answer:
The second Krark, the Thumbless trigger still resolves and you still flip a coin — but the outcomes differ because Song of Totentanz is no longer on the stack.

- If you lose the second flip: nothing happens. Song of Totentanz isn't on the stack anymore, so there's nothing to return; the card simply stays in your hand where the first trigger put it [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #4].
- If you win the second flip: a copy of Song of Totentanz is still created on the stack, even though the original spell has left the stack [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #12]. The copy keeps the same value of X that was chosen when Song of Totentanz was cast [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #3], so it creates that many 1/1 black Rat tokens with "This token can't block" and gives creatures you control haste. Note the copy isn't cast, so cast-triggers (including Krark's own) don't trigger again [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #2] — meaning the copy won't cause more coin flips.

Why there are two triggers at all: Spark Double entered as a copy of Krark, the Thumbless but is explicitly not legendary, and that exception is copiable, so the legend rule doesn't apply and both permanents exist with the flip ability [Spark Double ruling #6]. Each triggered separately on casting Song of Totentanz.

Also note that returning Song of Totentanz to hand is not countering it — it's removed from the stack and won't resolve [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #14], so the original never produces Rats; only a winning second flip can.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players, since all of it happens under Athena's control; the only multiplayer-relevant wrinkle is targeting/haste, and Song of Totentanz affects only creatures Athena controls when it resolves [Song of Totentanz ruling #0].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: If Athena loses the flip, nothing happens. If Athena wins the flip, a copy of Song of Totentanz is created.

entries.question: Alden cast [Ixidron]. Natalie controls a very cute [Tangled Florahedron]. What happens to it?
entries.reason: The candidate says Tangled Florahedron is turned face down by Ixidron, but the correct ruling is that Tangled Florahedron cannot be turned face down so nothing happens.
entries.answer:
Natalie's Tangled Florahedron gets turned face down as Ixidron enters the battlefield. Because Tangled Florahedron is a nontoken creature already on the battlefield, Ixidron's replacement effect ("As this creature enters, turn all other nontoken creatures face down") applies to it.

What that means concretely: Tangled Florahedron becomes a 2/2 face-down creature with no name, no text, no subtypes, no expansion symbol, and no mana cost, so it loses its "{T}: Add {G}" mana ability while face down [Ixidron ruling #4]. Natalie may still look at it any time, other players may not, but it must remain easily differentiable from her other face-down permanents so everyone can track which card it is [Ixidron ruling #2]. It also counts toward Ixidron's power and toughness, since Ixidron is */* equal to the number of face-down creatures on the battlefield.

Timing note: the turning face down happens *as* Ixidron enters — there is never a moment where Ixidron is on the battlefield with Tangled Florahedron face up, so a "whenever another creature enters" trigger on Tangled Florahedron (it has none) wouldn't see Ixidron [Ixidron ruling #3]. This is a replacement effect modifying how Ixidron enters; if other replacement effects also applied, the affected object's controller picks the order [616.1f], [614.12].

One exception: if Tangled Florahedron were entering the battlefield at the same time as Ixidron rather than already being there, it would enter face up and be unaffected [Ixidron ruling #1].

The answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game — Ixidron affects all other nontoken creatures regardless of controller. Note that if Natalie had instead played the card as its back face, Tangled Vale, it would be a land and not a creature, so Ixidron would leave it alone.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Nothing. Tangled Florahedron cannot be turned face down.

entries.question: Amani controls [Leyline of the Void] and casts [Hypnotic Cloud] to have Nicolas discard a card. Nicolas discards [Loxodon Smiter]. Does it end up on the battlefield or in exile?
entries.reason: The correct ruling is that Nicolas chooses which replacement effect applies (so it could be either), but the candidate incorrectly insists it will end up on the battlefield rather than saying the owner chooses.
entries.answer:
Loxodon Smiter ends up on the battlefield under Nicolas's control — Nicolas gets to choose, and he will apply Loxodon Smiter's own replacement effect, which sends it to the battlefield instead of the graveyard, so Leyline of the Void's graveyard-to-exile replacement never gets a chance to apply.

Why: Loxodon Smiter says "If a spell or ability an opponent controls causes you to discard this card, put it onto the battlefield instead of putting it into your graveyard." Hypnotic Cloud is a spell an opponent (Amani) controls that causes Nicolas to discard, so that condition is met. Discarding means moving the card from its owner's hand to that player's graveyard [Discard]. Two replacement effects want to modify that same graveyard event: Loxodon Smiter's (to the battlefield) and Leyline of the Void's ("If a card would be put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, exile it instead"). When multiple replacement effects could apply to one such zone-change event, the affected player chooses one to apply first — here that's Nicolas, the card's owner, exactly as in the example in [712.21d] where the affected player chooses which of Leyline of the Void's or the other effect's replacement to apply. Nicolas applies Loxodon Smiter's effect; the card is now heading to the battlefield, not to a graveyard, so Leyline of the Void's effect no longer has an event to replace and the card is not exiled. It enters under Nicolas's control, since an effect putting an object onto the battlefield does so under that player's control [110.2a].

(If Nicolas instead chose Leyline of the Void's effect, the card would go to exile and Loxodon Smiter's effect would then have nothing to replace — but the choice is his, and no rule forces him to pick that one.)

Note also that Nicolas has still discarded a card either way, so "whenever a player discards" triggers and madness-style abilities still work [Loxodon Smiter ruling #0], [Leyline of the Void ruling #2].

Multiplayer: nothing here changes with more than two players. Leyline of the Void only cares that the card's owner is an opponent of Amani, and Hypnotic Cloud targets a single player, so the same analysis applies at any table size.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Whichever Nicolas prefers. There are two replacement effects applying to Loxodon Smiter going to the graveyard. Nicolas is the controller of the affected object, so they choose where it ends up.

entries.question: In a Commander game with 4 players, Ari casts [Kardur, Doomscourge]. Bode controls [Oxidda Finisher], and [Parhelion II], which is not a creature at the time Kardur, Doomscourge's enter the battlefield ability resolves. During Bode's next turn, can they attack Ari with Parhelion II? Can they have the Angel tokens created by Parhelion II attack Ari?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling: Parhelion II (as a creature) must attack a player other than Ari, but the Angel tokens are created already attacking and Bode may choose Ari as their defending player.
entries.answer:
Direct answer: No — Bode can't attack Ari with Parhelion II once it's crewed; but yes, Bode may choose Ari as the player the two Angel tokens are attacking.

Why Parhelion II can't attack Ari: Kardur, Doomscourge's triggered ability says that until Ari's next turn, creatures Ari's opponents control attack each combat if able and attack a player other than Ari if able. That's a continuously applied restriction on all creatures those opponents control, not a one-shot snapshot of the battlefield at resolution — Kardur, Doomscourge ruling #2 confirms it affects creatures that come to be there after the ability resolves. Parhelion II was a noncreature Vehicle when the ability resolved, but if Bode crews it (Crew 4) during Bode's turn it becomes an artifact creature Bode controls, and the requirement then applies to it. In a 4-player Commander game Bode has two other opponents to attack and no attack-left/attack-right restriction is in use by default, so Parhelion II is able to attack a player other than Ari and therefore must ([508.1b], Kardur, Doomscourge ruling #0, ruling #3 — Bode chooses which of the other players or their planeswalkers/battles). Note Oxidda Finisher is likewise forced to attack and to attack someone other than Ari if able (Kardur, Doomscourge ruling #4 covers the cases where a creature simply can't attack, e.g. tapped).

Why the Angel tokens can attack Ari: Parhelion II's trigger creates the two 4/4 Angels already attacking. They are put onto the battlefield attacking rather than declared as attackers, so Bode chooses which defending player, planeswalker, or battle each one is attacking as it enters ([508.4a], [508.4b], Parhelion II ruling #0). Such creatures are "attacking" but never "attacked" (Parhelion II ruling #1), so Kardur, Doomscourge's declare-attackers requirement to attack a player other than Ari never constrains that choice — Bode may point one or both Angels at Ari. They also needn't attack the same player as Parhelion II.

Only a player, planeswalker, or battle can be attacked in the first place ([506.3]). Because this is a 4-player game, the "attack a player other than you if able" clause has real bite; in a two-player game Ari would be Bode's only opponent, so the clause would do nothing and Parhelion II could attack Ari (or Ari's planeswalkers/battles) as per Kardur, Doomscourge ruling #0.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Parhelion II is crewed during Bode's turn while Kardur, Doomscourge's effect is still active (it lasts until Ari's next turn). If Parhelion II somehow attacks after that duration ends, no attack requirement or restriction applies at all and it could attack Ari freely.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Bode cannot attack Ari with Parhelion II, but they can choose for the Angel tokens to attack Ari.

Kardur, Doomscourge's enters-the-battlefield ability sets up a rules change that causes any creatures Ari's opponents control to have to attack if able and to have to attack another player if able. Since this is a change in the rules of the game, it affects Parhelion II even if it is not a creature at the time the ability resolves.

The Angel tokens are created attacking, but are never declared as attackers. Because of this, Bode can choose Ari to be the defending player for the tokens.

entries.question: Aislinn controls two [Bramblewood Paragon]s and casts [Thunder-Thrash Elder]. What is the maximum amount of counters Thunder-Thrash Elder can enter the battlefield with?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling — Thunder‑Thrash Elder can enter with up to eight +1/+1 counters (6 from devour plus 2 from the two Bramblewood Paragons).
entries.answer:
With only those two Bramblewood Paragons on the battlefield, Thunder-Thrash Elder can enter with a maximum of 8 +1/+1 counters: 6 from devour 3 (sacrificing both Bramblewood Paragons, 3 counters each) plus 2 more from the two Bramblewood Paragons' replacement effects.

How this works:
- Thunder-Thrash Elder is a Lizard **Warrior**, so each Bramblewood Paragon's ability applies, and the effects of more than one Bramblewood Paragon are cumulative — two Bramblewood Paragons mean two additional +1/+1 counters [Bramblewood Paragon ruling #1], [Bramblewood Paragon ruling #2].
- Devour 3 lets you sacrifice any number of creatures already on the battlefield as Thunder-Thrash Elder enters; it can't devour itself or anything entering alongside it [Thunder-Thrash Elder ruling #0]. Both Bramblewood Paragons are legal sacrifices, giving 3 counters each = 6.
- All of these are replacement effects modifying how Thunder-Thrash Elder enters the battlefield, applied as a single event; the two Bramblewood Paragons are still on the battlefield when their abilities apply, so their bonus counters still count. Note that the same object can't be chosen to change zones more than once when applying these entry-modifying replacement effects, so each Bramblewood Paragon can only be devoured once [614.13b].
- Counters given as a permanent enters count as counters put on it, and Thunder-Thrash Elder's controller (Aislinn) puts them on [122.6a].

If Aislinn controls other creatures too, the total is 3 × (number of creatures devoured) + 2; the "8" figure assumes the two Bramblewood Paragons are her only other creatures. Devouring is optional, so she could also choose 0 sacrifices and enter with just 2 counters [Thunder-Thrash Elder ruling #3].

Nothing here depends on player count, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Eight. Both Bramblewood Paragon and Thunder-Thrash Elder have replacement effects that modify how Thunder-Thrash Elder enters the battlefield. While Thunder-Thrash Elder is entering the battlefield the game checks which replacement effects to apply, and sees that there are two Bramblewood Paragons that want to place an additional +1/+1 counter on Thunder-Thrash Elder as well as a Devour ability. If Aislinn chooses to devour the Bramblewood Paragons, they will place an additional six +1/+1 counters on Thunder-Thrash Elder.

entries.question: Is [Umori, the Collector] a legal companion for a deck containing only [Grist, the Hunger Tide], creatures, and lands?
entries.reason: Both conclude Umori is legal because Grist's static ability makes it a creature in every zone (including before the game), so all nonland cards in the deck share the creature type.
entries.answer:
Yes. Umori, the Collector is a legal companion for that deck. Umori, the Collector's companion condition is "Each nonland card in your starting deck shares a card type," and here the shared card type is creature: Grist, the Hunger Tide has the static ability "As long as Grist isn't on the battlefield, it's a 1/1 Insect creature in addition to its other types," which works in every zone other than the battlefield — including during deck construction. Anywhere but the battlefield, Grist, the Hunger Tide is a Legendary Planeswalker Creature — Grist Insect [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #3], and that ability functions before the game begins [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #2]. So Grist, the Hunger Tide has the creature card type just like the rest of your nonland cards, satisfying Umori, the Collector [Umori, the Collector ruling #1]. Land cards are ignored for this check and may have any extra types [Umori, the Collector ruling #4].

Definitions/details:
- Companion is a keyword ability functioning outside the game: before the game you may reveal one card you own from outside the game whose companion condition your starting deck fulfills, and once during the game, with priority during your main phase and an empty stack, pay {3} as a special action to put it into your hand [702.139a] [103.2b] [Companion].
- "Starting deck" means your deck after setting aside sideboard cards, and in Commander, before setting aside your commander — so your commander counts toward the condition, and the companion itself is not one of your 100 cards [702.139b] [Umori, the Collector ruling #7].
- If Grist, the Hunger Tide is your commander, color identity also checks out: Grist, the Hunger Tide's color identity is black-green, and Umori, the Collector's mana cost {2}{B/G}{B/G} gives it a black-green color identity, so it's legal to bring in from outside the game [903.4] [903.11a] [702.139d].
- Note the shared type must be one type every nonland card has; if any of your "creatures" were, say, a pure artifact or enchantment noncreature, the condition would fail [Umori, the Collector ruling #1].

Multiplayer note: this is a deck-construction/pregame matter and doesn't change with player count, except that if several players want to reveal companions, the starting player reveals first and play proceeds in turn order [Umori, the Collector ruling #2].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Grist, the Hunger Tide's ability is in effect even before the game begins..

entries.question: Abel crews their [Adrestia]. Nathalie activates their [Mobilized District] causing it to become a creature. After that resolves, Nathalie casts [Mirrorweave] targeting their Mobilized District. What are Adrestia's characteristics after Mirrorweave resolves?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly concludes Adrestia becomes a noncreature land, whereas the correct ruling is it remains an artifact creature from the crew continuous effect and thus is a 0/0 artifact creature with Mobilized District's abilities.
entries.answer:
After Mirrorweave resolves, Abel's Adrestia becomes a copy of Mobilized District's printed values only — so it is a noncreature land named Mobilized District until end of turn.

Why: Adrestia was crewed, so it was an artifact creature and therefore "each other creature" for Mirrorweave (Mirrorweave hits every other creature; the legendary restriction applies only to the target, and Nathalie's Mobilized District is nonlegendary). A copy effect copies only copiable values — the values from the printed text (name, mana cost, color indicator, card types, subtypes, supertypes, rules text, power/toughness) as modified by other copy effects — not type-changing or other continuous effects, counters, or status [707.2, 707.2a, 613.1a, 613.2a]. Mobilized District's {4} ability that animated it is a type-changing/P-T-setting effect, not a copiable value, so it isn't copied [Mirrorweave ruling #0, Mirrorweave ruling #5].

So Adrestia now has: name Mobilized District; no mana cost; colorless (no mana cost or color indicator); card type Land only (not legendary, not an artifact, not a Vehicle, not a creature); no power or toughness; and the abilities "{T}: Add {C}" and "{4}: This land becomes a 3/3 Citizen creature with vigilance until end of turn. It's still a land. This ability costs {1} less to activate for each legendary creature and planeswalker you control." It loses islandwalk, the attack-trigger ability, and Crew 1. Note {C} is colorless mana specifically, not generic.

Because it is no longer a creature, the crew effect is irrelevant while Mirrorweave's effect lasts (Adrestia isn't attacking or blocking, and it isn't tapped by crewing). Abel could activate the copied {4} ability to animate it as a 3/3 Citizen land, and Abel's own legendary creatures/planeswalkers would reduce that generic cost [Mobilized District ruling #0]. At end of turn Mirrorweave's effect wears off and it is Adrestia again [Mirrorweave ruling #3]; any crew effect from this turn will also have expired.

One assumption: Adrestia was still crewed (a creature) when Mirrorweave resolved. If Adrestia had not been crewed, it wouldn't be a creature and Mirrorweave would not affect it at all. Nothing here depends on the number of players — Mirrorweave affects every other creature on the battlefield regardless of controller, so with more opponents every other creature likewise becomes an unanimated Mobilized District.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
It's a 0/0 colorless land artifact creature with no subtypes and the abilities of Mobilized District.

When Adrestia becomes a copy of Mobilized District, it copies only the copiable values of the permanent, which does not include continuous effects like the one turning Mobilized District into a creature.

The effect from crew is still making Adrestia an artifact creature ([702.122a]), but it doesn't define a power and toughness, so the game treats it as 0/0.

entries.question: Ari controls a [Lunarch Inquisitors] that exiled a [Jasmine Boreal] when it transformed. Nyla casts [Moonmist]. Does the Jasmine Boreal return to the battlefield?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that transforming Lunarch Inquisitors does not cause the exiled Jasmine Boreal to return—the exile lasts until the permanent actually leaves the battlefield.
entries.answer:
No — Jasmine Boreal stays in exile. Moonmist transforms all Humans, and Lunarch Inquisitors is a Human Cleric represented by a double-faced card, so it transforms back into Avacynian Missionaries. But transforming is not the same as leaving the battlefield: the exile effect lasts "until this creature leaves the battlefield," and the permanent is still the same permanent on the battlefield after transforming. As the card's own rulings state, if Lunarch Inquisitors somehow transforms into Avacynian Missionaries, the exiled creature remains exiled; if Avacynian Missionaries later leaves the battlefield, Jasmine Boreal returns to the battlefield then [Avacynian Missionaries // Lunarch Inquisitors ruling #5]. Because that return is a second one-shot effect created immediately after the "leaves the battlefield" event, and it returns the card under its owner's control [610.3c].

A couple of side notes: Jasmine Boreal is itself a Human, but it's in the exile zone, not on the battlefield, so Moonmist doesn't affect it (and it isn't a double-faced card, so it couldn't transform anyway) [712.9]. Moonmist also prevents all combat damage this turn from creatures other than Werewolves and Wolves, checked as damage is dealt [Moonmist ruling #0].

Multiplayer difference: with more than two players, if Ari (the owner of Lunarch Inquisitors) leaves the game, the exiled Jasmine Boreal does return to the battlefield, because the returning one-shot effect isn't an ability on the stack and so doesn't cease to exist with the departing player's spells and abilities [Avacynian Missionaries // Lunarch Inquisitors ruling #3]. In a two-player game the game simply ends instead.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Whenever a card refers to itself by name, it just means "this object". The exiled creature will return to the battlefield only when the permanent that was Lunarch Inquisitors leaves the battlefield, regardless of which face it was on at that time.

entries.question: Addison controls [Carth the Lion] and [Bioessence Hydra]. Addison activates the [+1] ability of [Dovin, Architect of Law]. How many times does Bioessence Hydra trigger?
entries.reason: Both conclude the extra loyalty cost from Carth combines into a single event that puts two counters on Dovin, producing one Bioessence Hydra trigger that grants two +1/+1 counters.
entries.answer:
Bioessence Hydra triggers exactly once, and that single trigger puts two +1/+1 counters on Bioessence Hydra.

Why: Carth the Lion's static ability says "Planeswalkers' loyalty abilities you activate cost an additional [+1] to activate," so Dovin, Architect of Law's [+1] ability costs [+2] instead ([Carth the Lion ruling #3]). Multiple loyalty-counter costs are combined into a single cost to add counters (606.5), and the total is calculated before any counters are added — you don't add one, then another ([Carth the Lion ruling #0]). So paying the cost is one event in which two loyalty counters are put on Dovin, Architect of Law at the same time.

Bioessence Hydra's last ability reads "Whenever one or more loyalty counters are put on planeswalkers you control, put that many +1/+1 counters on this creature." Because it keys on "one or more" counters in a single event, one event of two counters means one trigger for two +1/+1 counters, not two triggers.

This is unaffected by the number of players at the table; loyalty costs and Bioessence Hydra's trigger work the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Side note: if Addison somehow controlled two Carth the Lions, the cost increase is cumulative to [+3] total counters ([Carth the Lion ruling #1]) — still one Bioessence Hydra trigger, for three +1/+1 counters.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Once. If a planeswalker's ability has multiple costs to add or remove loyalty counters, those costs are combined into a single cost.

entries.question: Nico casts [Assert Authority] targeting Ainsley's [Blightsteel Colossus]. What happens as Assert Authority resolves?
entries.reason: The candidate says the card's controller chooses whether it's exiled or shuffled, but the reference states Assert Authority's replacement is applied first so the Colossus is countered and exiled, not chosen by Ainsley.
entries.answer:
Assert Authority counters Blightsteel Colossus, but where the countered card ends up is Ainsley's choice, not Nico's. Two replacement effects are trying to modify the same event (the countered spell being put into its owner's graveyard): Assert Authority's "exile it instead of putting it into its owner's graveyard," and Blightsteel Colossus's own "If Blightsteel Colossus would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, reveal Blightsteel Colossus and shuffle it into its owner's library instead." Because Blightsteel Colossus is the affected object and Ainsley controls/owns it, Ainsley picks which replacement to apply; once one is applied the event no longer involves the graveyard, so the other does nothing [616.1f]. So either Blightsteel Colossus is exiled, or it is revealed and shuffled into Ainsley's library — Ainsley decides.

Notes: Blightsteel Colossus's indestructible does nothing here; countering isn't destruction, and Blightsteel Colossus is still a spell on the stack, not a permanent. Its printed replacement ability applies "from anywhere," including the stack, and that card text is what creates the competing replacement rather than any general rule [616.1f].

On cost, for completeness: Assert Authority costs {5}{U}{U}, and affinity for artifacts reduces only the generic portion — with, say, three artifacts Nico pays {2}{U}{U}; the {U}{U} can never be reduced.

This works the same at a two-player table or in multiplayer; the choice always belongs to the countered spell's controller (Ainsley). If several players had simultaneous choices to make, they'd be made in APNAP order [616.1f].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Blightsteel Colossus will be countered and exiled. Because Assert Authority has a self-replacement effect, it has to be chosen first before Blightsteel Colossus's replacement effect. Because Blightsteel Colossus is no longer going to the graveyard, its replacement effect can no longer apply.

entries.question: Amani has 3 life. Briar casts [Chain of Plasma], targeting Amani. As it resolves, Amani pays the cost to copy it, and chooses to have the copy target Campbell. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate fails to state that the copy is removed from the stack when Amani loses the game after the original finishes resolving, leaving the copy's fate ambiguous instead of matching the reference ruling.
entries.answer:
Direct answer: Chain of Plasma resolves and deals 3 damage to Amani, dropping Amani to 0 life. Amani still gets to finish the resolution — a spell's resolution isn't interrupted, and the copy is created during that resolution — so Amani may discard a card and copy Chain of Plasma, choosing Campbell as the copy's new target. That copy is a new spell on the stack, owned and controlled by Amani ([707.10]), and it will deal 3 damage to Campbell if it resolves. Only after Chain of Plasma finishes resolving is Amani's 0 life noticed, and Amani loses the game.

Details:
- The 3 damage is processed into life loss as part of the damage event ([120.4c]).
- The copy copies all of Chain of Plasma's characteristics and choices, except that Amani, as the copy's controller, changes the target to Campbell; the new target must be legal ([707.10], [707.10c]).
- Chain of Plasma's own text is what grants this: the damaged player "may discard a card. If the player does, they may copy this spell and may choose a new target for that copy" — so the copier is Amani, not Briar.

What happens to the copy after Amani loses: in a two-player game (Briar and Amani, with Campbell being a third player, so this is a multiplayer game as described), Amani leaving the game normally removes objects Amani owns/controls from the stack — but the rules provided here don't include the rule about a player leaving the game and its effect on the stack, so I can't confirm that outcome from this context. If a two-player game somehow ended when Amani hit 0 life, nothing further would resolve. Note also that if any redirection effect were involved and Amani had already left the game, that redirection would simply do nothing ([614.9]).

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Amani chooses to discard immediately during Chain of Plasma's resolution, as the card directs. There is no window for anyone to act between the damage and the discard/copy, since both happen during the same resolution.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The copy is put onto the stack targeting Campbell. Then the original Chain of Plasma finishes resolving and state-based actions are checked. Amani loses the game, and the copy of Chain of Plasma is removed from the stack before it would resolve.

entries.question: In a multiplayer game, Achilles uses [Jon Irenicus, Shattered One] to give [Vastwood Gorger] to Brynn. If Brynn dies, what happens to Vastwood Gorger?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling that Brynn's control-ending causes Vastwood Gorger to revert to its owner Achilles and remain on the battlefield.
entries.answer:
Vastwood Gorger returns to Achilles' control and stays on the battlefield.

Why: Achilles owns Vastwood Gorger — Jon Irenicus, Shattered One only gave Brynn control of it, not ownership. When a player leaves a multiplayer game, all objects owned by that player leave the game with them, and any effects giving that player control of objects end [800.4a]. Since the control-change effect from Jon Irenicus, Shattered One ends, Vastwood Gorger reverts to its owner Achilles, who is still in the game, so it simply remains on the battlefield under Achilles' control. This happens immediately as Brynn leaves the game, not as a state-based action.

It is not exiled: exile only applies to objects still controlled by the departing player (i.e., ones they own or whose default controller has left the game) [800.4a] [800.4c]. Here the default controller/owner, Achilles, is still in the game.

The +1/+1 counters Jon Irenicus, Shattered One placed stay on Vastwood Gorger, and the granted ability "This creature can't be sacrificed" and the goad effect ("goaded for the rest of the game") continue to apply, since those were not dependent on Brynn's presence — though goad has no practical effect while Vastwood Gorger is back under Achilles' own control unless another player gains control of it later.

Note on "dies": a creature or planeswalker "dies" when it's put into a graveyard from the battlefield [700.4] [Dies]; players don't "die" — I'm reading your question as Brynn losing and leaving the game. This whole scenario is multiplayer-specific; in a two-player game, one player leaving ends the game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Achilles gets their Vastwood Gorger back. When Brynn leaves the game, any effects giving them control of any objects end.

entries.question: Aspen attacks with [Hammers of Moradin]. During the combat damage step, they use [Time Stop] to end the turn. What happens to the tokens created by myriad?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes the tokens are never exiled, while the reference states they remain and will be exiled at the beginning of the next end of combat step, so the rulings conflict.
entries.answer:
The myriad tokens stay on the battlefield permanently — they're never exiled.

Why: Hammers of Moradin's myriad creates token copies that are tapped and attacking, plus a delayed triggered ability that exiles those tokens "at end of combat" [702.116a]. An "at end of combat" ability triggers as the end of combat step begins [511.2]. Time Stop ends the turn: all spells and abilities on the stack are exiled, all attacking and blocking creatures are removed from combat, the current step (here, the combat damage step) ends, and the game skips straight to the cleanup step, skipping every phase or step in between [724.1d, Time Stop ruling #3]. Because the end of combat step never begins, the delayed "exile the tokens" trigger never triggers at all, so nothing exiles them. Any abilities that had already triggered but weren't yet on the stack simply cease to exist [724.1a].

So after the turn ends you're left with Aspen's token copies of Hammers of Moradin on the battlefield, no longer attacking (removed from combat), with damage removed and "until end of turn" effects ended during the cleanup step [514.2, 703.4p]. They are ordinary tokens from then on and persist into future turns.

Timing note: I'm assuming Time Stop resolved during the combat damage step, before the end of combat step began, as stated. If instead it resolved after the end of combat step had already begun, the exile trigger would have already triggered — and if it were still waiting to go on the stack when Time Stop began ending the turn, it would cease to exist [724.1a]; if it had already resolved, the tokens would already be in exile.

Multiplayer: myriad only makes tokens for opponents other than the defending player, so this scenario requires at least three players (with only one opponent, no tokens are created at all) [Hammers of Moradin ruling #3]. The outcome for each token is the same regardless of how many opponents there are.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: They remain on the battlefield, and will be exiled at the beginning of the next end of combat step. ([702.116a], [511.2], [603.7b])

entries.question: If Avery is going first, they'd like to reveal [Umori, the Collector] as their companion. If they're going second, they don't want to have a companion. Can they do this?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the same ruling: the starting player is chosen before the companion-reveal step, so Avery can reveal Umori when going first and decline when going second.
entries.answer:
Yes. Revealing a companion happens after the starting player has been determined, so Avery already knows whether they're going first when they decide whether to reveal Umori, the Collector.

Details:
- Rule 103.2b lists revealing a companion among the additional start-of-game steps performed *after* the starting player is chosen. So the information Avery wants to condition on (going first or not) is available before the choice.
- Companion means: before the game begins you may reveal one card you own from outside the game whose companion condition is met by your starting deck; later, once per game, you may pay {3} as a special action to put it into your hand (rules 702.139a, 116.2g). Umori, the Collector's condition is that each nonland card in Avery's starting deck shares a card type (Umori, the Collector ruling #1, #4).
- Avery must still legally satisfy that condition with their starting deck (after setting aside sideboard cards, per 702.139b) in order to reveal Umori, the Collector at all — the choice to skip it is always allowed, but the choice to reveal requires the deck to qualify.
- Order of the reveal step: the starting player declares first, then players proceed in turn order, and once a player declines they can't change their mind (Umori, the Collector ruling #2). This matters in multiplayer just as in a two-player game: if Avery isn't first, they'll declare at their spot in turn order, possibly after seeing some opponents' choices, and can simply decline. With more than two players the only difference is how many players declare before Avery.

So the strategy is fully legal: reveal Umori, the Collector when on the play, decline when on the draw.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Starting player is determined before Avery would need to reveal their companion.

entries.answer:
Aspen draws zero cards, then discards three cards.

Bane Alley Blackguard is a 1/3. Mystic Subdual gives the enchanted creature -2/-0, so Bane Alley Blackguard's power on the battlefield was -1 (1 - 2). Greater Good's ability uses the sacrificed creature's power as it last existed on the battlefield [Greater Good ruling #0], so the instruction is to draw -1 cards. Magic only uses integers and a draw instruction can't be a negative number of cards, so it's treated as drawing zero — an effect does only as much as possible [107.1c, 609.3].

The discard is not optional or tied to the draw: Greater Good still says "then discard three cards," so Aspen discards three cards from hand (or their entire hand if they have fewer than three) [Greater Good ruling #1]. All of this happens during the resolution of Greater Good's ability, so no player can act in between [Greater Good ruling #2].

Note also that Mystic Subdual makes Bane Alley Blackguard lose all abilities, but that's irrelevant here since Greater Good's ability is doing the sacrificing, not an ability of Bane Alley Blackguard.

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players at the table.
