entries.answer_gold: None. The players first draw seven cards each, triggering Sheoldred, the Apocalypse fourteen times. Then Alessandra ends the turn, which nullifies those triggers before they're even put onto the stack.

entries.question: It is currently day and Adonis controls [Lazotep Convert] (the back face of [Invasion of Amonkhet]), which is a copy of [Kessig Naturalist]. What happens if it becomes night?
entries.reason: Both conclude Lazotep Convert remains a back-face-up copy of Kessig Naturalist and does not transform at night because the daybound transform only applies to front-face-up permanents.
entries.answer:
Nothing happens to it — Lazotep Convert stays exactly as it is, a back-face-up permanent that's a copy of Kessig Naturalist.

Why: daybound is not simply "transform when it becomes night." It means "If it is night and this permanent is represented by a double-faced card, it enters transformed," "As it becomes night, if this permanent is front face up, transform it," and "This permanent can't transform except due to its daybound ability" [702.145b]. Adonis's permanent is the back face (Lazotep Convert) of the transforming double-faced card Invasion of Amonkhet // Lazotep Convert, so it is not front face up. The transform clause simply doesn't apply, and the ongoing check in [702.145c] (which also only catches permanents that are front face up with daybound while it's night) likewise finds nothing to do.

The mirror-image rule [702.145f], which transforms back-face-up permanents during day, only applies to permanents with nightbound. Because Lazotep Convert copied the creature card Kessig Naturalist, it has Kessig Naturalist's printed abilities, including daybound — it does not gain Lord of the Ulvenwald's nightbound [Kessig Naturalist // Lord of the Ulvenwald ruling #8, Invasion of Amonkhet // Lazotep Convert ruling #12]. So there is no nightbound ability to make it flip either, and the "can't transform except due to its daybound ability" clause blocks any other transform effect [702.145b].

One practical note: if it somehow did transform, it would turn into Invasion of Amonkhet, a Siege with no defense counters, which would then be put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action [Invasion of Amonkhet // Lazotep Convert ruling #14, Invasion of Amonkhet // Lazotep Convert ruling #9]. That doesn't happen here.

Timing/assumption: I'm assuming the standard way it becomes night — the untap-step day/night check, e.g. day plus the previous turn's active player casting no spells [502.2], [731.2a]. The answer is the same no matter when or how it becomes night, since the transform clause keys on the permanent being front face up [Kessig Naturalist // Lord of the Ulvenwald ruling #2].

Player count doesn't change this. The day/night check looks at the previous turn's single active player [731.2a], [731.2b], so with more than two players the same rule applies to whoever took the previous turn; the effect on Lazotep Convert is unchanged.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Lazotep Convert will be a copy of Kessig Naturalist. As it becomes night, it will not transform and remain a copy of Kessig Naturalist. Lazotep Convert will only copy the front face of Kessig Naturalist and does not copy its status. When it becomes night, it will not transform because a daybound permanent will only transform as it becomes night if it is front face up. ([702.145b])

entries.question: Adelina's [Fireblade Charger] dies, and Nasir responds with [Thwart the Enemy]. Is the damage prevented?
entries.reason: The candidate gives a definitive "yes" that the damage is prevented (with a timing caveat), while the reference states the outcome is unclear and not conclusively settled.
entries.answer:
Yes — the damage is prevented, assuming Nasir casts Thwart the Enemy while Fireblade Charger's death trigger is still on the stack (i.e., it resolves before that trigger resolves).

Why: "Prevent" means the damage simply never happens (615.6, Prevent glossary), and prevention effects act as shields that must already exist when the damage event would occur (615.4). Fireblade Charger's triggered ability ("When this creature dies, it deals damage equal to its power to any target") uses Fireblade Charger itself as the damage source, and its last known information on the battlefield is used, including its power (Fireblade Charger ruling #0). That last known information is a creature Adelina controls, so when the shield rechecks the source's properties at the moment damage would be dealt, Fireblade Charger still matches "creatures your opponents control" (609.7b, 615.9). Rule 609.7c also confirms that effects prevented from sources with a given property apply to sources that aren't on the battlefield but have that property.

Timing caveat: if Nasir instead waits until Fireblade Charger's trigger has already resolved and the damage has been dealt, Thwart the Enemy comes too late — prevention effects can't go back in time (615.4). Note also that Thwart the Enemy does not stop the death trigger from triggering or resolving; it only stops the damage. Since all the damage is prevented, anything that would trigger on that damage being dealt (like lifelink-style or "deals damage" triggers) does not trigger (603.2g).

Multiplayer: Thwart the Enemy says "creatures your opponents control," so it covers Fireblade Charger no matter how many opponents are at the table, as long as Adelina is Nasir's opponent; the answer is the same in a two-player game or a bigger table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Unclear. Fireblade Charger is not currently a creature on the battlefield, but the game uses its last known information to determine how the damage is dealt. If Fireblade Charger only applies to objects that are creatures, like how Biomantic Mastery only counts creatures that actually exist on the battlefield, it won't be prevented. But if Fireblade Charger checks the source of damage to see whether it's a creature, it will be able to identify the damage as coming from a creature. The intention is probably the latter, but Wizards has not clarified.

entries.question: Nico controls Analia's [Bane Alley Blackguard] enchanted with their [Corrupted Conscience]. Analia casts their own [Lay Claim], targeting Nico's Corrupted Conscience. After it resolves, who controls the Bane Alley Blackguard? Who controls the Corrupted Conscience?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Lay Claim causes Analia to control Corrupted Conscience and then Corrupted Conscience causes Analia to control Bane Alley Blackguard, so Analia ends up controlling all three permanents.
entries.answer:
Analia ends up controlling everything: Lay Claim, Corrupted Conscience, and Bane Alley Blackguard.

Why: Lay Claim reads "Enchant permanent / You control enchanted permanent," and Corrupted Conscience is itself a permanent (an Aura enchantment), so it's a legal target. Once Analia's Lay Claim is attached, Analia is the controller of Corrupted Conscience — an Aura's controller is tracked separately from the controller of what it enchants, and control of the two can differ (303.4e). Corrupted Conscience then says "You control enchanted creature," and "you" means its current controller, Analia. So Analia gains control of Bane Alley Blackguard as well (and, being the card's owner, has it back under her control).

Ordering note: both are continuous control-changing effects applied in layer 2 (613.1b), and they aren't in conflict — Lay Claim's effect determines who "you" is for Corrupted Conscience, and Corrupted Conscience's effect then hands Bane Alley Blackguard to that player. Nico controls none of the three permanents afterward; Nico still owns the Corrupted Conscience card, but ownership and control are different things (110.2b). Note also that Nico's control of Bane Alley Blackguard only ever came from Corrupted Conscience, so redirecting the Aura's control redirects the creature too.

This analysis is the same whether the game has two players or more; nothing here depends on player count. One multiplayer wrinkle worth knowing: if a player leaves the game, control effects granting them objects end and Aura-based control reverts (800.4a) — e.g., if Analia left, Lay Claim would leave with her and Corrupted Conscience would revert to Nico's control, giving Bane Alley Blackguard back to Nico.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Analia controls both permanents. Out of the two auras, Corrupted Conscience has the earlier timestamp, and would normally be applied first. However, the effects from both auras apply in the same layer, applying the Lay Claim's effect would change how the Corrupted Conscience's effect is applied, and applying the Corrupted Conscience's effect would not change how the Lay Claim's effect is applied, so the Corrupted Conscience's effect is dependent on the Lay Claim's effect. The Lay Claim's effect applies first, giving Analia control of Corrupted Conscience, and then the Corrupted Conscience's effect applies, giving Analia control of Bane Alley Blackguard.

entries.question: Autumn controls [Traveling Chocobo] and casts [Phyrexian Ingester]. Autumn exiles [Scarwood Goblins] and then [Tor Giant] with the triggers. What are Phyrexian Ingester's power and toughness?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches a 5/5 conclusion by asserting Traveling Chocobo doesn't duplicate Phyrexian Ingester's imprint trigger, but the correct ruling is that both Scarwood Goblins and Tor Giant are exiled and Ingester becomes an 8/8.
entries.answer:
Phyrexian Ingester ends up 5/5 — and the premise doesn't actually happen: Traveling Chocobo does not give Phyrexian Ingester's imprint trigger an extra instance, so only one creature (Scarwood Goblins, the first target chosen) gets exiled.

Why: Traveling Chocobo's last ability reads "If a land or Bird you control entering the battlefield causes a triggered ability of a permanent you control to trigger, that ability triggers an additional time." Phyrexian Ingester is a Phyrexian Beast, not a land and not a Bird, so its own "When this creature enters, you may exile target nontoken creature" ability triggers only once (see [Traveling Chocobo ruling #12], which confirms the ability applies to a permanent's own "enters" triggers only as long as it's a land or Bird you control).

With one exiled card, Scarwood Goblins (a 2/2), Phyrexian Ingester's second ability gives it +2/+2. That's a power/toughness-modifying effect applied in layer 7c, on top of its printed 3/3 ([302.4c], [613.1g], [613.4c]), for 5/5. Tor Giant is never exiled and contributes nothing.

If you had somehow gotten two instances of the imprint trigger (for example if Phyrexian Ingester were a Bird), both Scarwood Goblins and Tor Giant would be exiled and "the exiled creature card's power/toughness" would give multiple answers whose sum is used, per [Traveling Chocobo ruling #8] — that would be +5/+5, making Phyrexian Ingester 8/8. Note also that the bonus uses the cards' values in exile, ignoring counters or Auras they had on the battlefield ([Phyrexian Ingester ruling #1]).

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
It's an 8/8.

The enter-the-battlefield ability of Phyrexian Ingester is part of a pair of linked abilities. When determining a value for Phyrexian Ingester's second ability, the sum of the powers and toughnesses from Scarwood Goblins and Tor Giant is used. This gives Phyrexian Ingester +5/+5, which makes it an 8/8.

entries.question: Beverly controls [Pandemonium]. Adalynn casts [Knight Errant] and targets Beverly's [Forest Bear] with the Pandemonium trigger. In response Channing casts [Ral's Outburst] targeting Adalynn causing them to lose the game. Will Beverly's creature die?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the Pandemonium trigger is controlled by Beverly and will result in the choice being made after Adalynn leaves (so the trigger can deal damage and the Forest Bear dies).
entries.answer:
Most likely yes — Beverly's Forest Bear takes 2 damage and dies, assuming the Pandemonium ability still does its damage.

How it plays out:

1. Beverly controls Pandemonium, so Beverly controls the Pandemonium triggered ability even though Adalynn's Knight Errant is the creature that entered and Adalynn is the one who picks the target and whether to have it deal damage [Pandemonium ruling #1]. Because Beverly (not Adalynn) controls the ability, it stays on the stack when Adalynn leaves the game.

2. Channing's Ral's Outburst was cast in response, so it resolves first and Adalynn loses the game [104.3e]. Any "whenever a player loses the game" triggers look back in time to the game state just before that event [603.9, 603.10f].

3. When Adalynn leaves, Adalynn's Knight Errant leaves the battlefield too. That does not fizzle the Pandemonium ability: Pandemonium's ability doesn't check the creature's power until it resolves, and if the creature is gone it uses the power the creature had immediately before it left the battlefield — 2 [Pandemonium ruling #0]. The target (Forest Bear) is still legal.

4. The Pandemonium ability resolves and deals 2 damage to Beverly's Forest Bear, a 2/2, which is lethal, so Forest Bear is destroyed.

One genuine wrinkle: the "may have it deal damage" choice is made on resolution by Adalynn, the entering creature's controller [Pandemonium ruling #1]. If you treat that choice as already locked in (which is how the question is framed — Adalynn "targets" and evidently opted in), Forest Bear dies. If you instead treat the choice as still pending at resolution, Adalynn is no longer in the game to make it, no one else may make it for them, and no damage is dealt — Forest Bear survives. The provided rules don't spell out that specific point.

Multiplayer note: this is already a three-player situation, and nothing here depends on player count except that Adalynn's departure removes Adalynn's permanents. In a game with limited range of influence, a trigger only functions if the event is within its controller's range [801.7a], but at a normal table everyone is in range.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The triggered ability of Pandemonium includes a choice to be made upon resolution. However the player that is supposed to make that choice is no longer in the game, therefore the controller of the trigger chooses another player to make that choice. In this case Beverly will choose another player to decide whether Pandemonium's trigger will deal damage to Forest Bear. Beverly is the controller of the trigger since they control the enchantment that generated the trigger, even though Adalynn is the player making choices about the trigger.

entries.question: Asher casts [Show and Tell]. As it resolves, Asher wants to put [Hall of Triumph] onto the battlefield. Do they know what Noa is putting onto the battlefield while making the choice for Hall of Triumph's replacement effect?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Yes — Show and Tell has each player choose their card before replacement/entering choices are made, so Asher will know which card Noa chose when choosing Hall of Triumph's color.
entries.answer:
Yes — by the time Asher chooses a color for Hall of Triumph, Noa has already chosen which card they're putting onto the battlefield.

How it works during Show and Tell's resolution:

1. Each player chooses a card first, in turn order: Asher (the active player, since they cast it) chooses, then Noa and any other players choose in turn order. A player doesn't have to reveal the chosen card as long as it's clear which card was chosen [Show and Tell ruling #2].
2. Only after all players have made those choices are the additional choices required by the cards themselves made — the active player makes choices for their card first, then the other players in turn order [Show and Tell ruling #0].

Hall of Triumph reads "As Hall of Triumph enters, choose a color," which is a replacement effect that modifies how the permanent enters the battlefield; that choice is made before it actually enters the battlefield [614.12a]. Since the card-selection step already finished, Asher knows what card Noa selected (at least that it's clear which card it is) when picking the color, consistent with the general principle that a player knows the choices made by previous players [101.4b]. Note, however, that Asher does not know a color or other choice Noa may make for Noa's own permanent, because Asher, as active player, makes their choice first [Show and Tell ruling #0]. All the cards then enter the battlefield simultaneously [Show and Tell ruling #2].

With more than two players the answer is the same, just extended: everyone picks a card in turn order starting with the active player, then per-card choices happen in that same order, so Asher knows every player's chosen card but none of their later choices.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Show and Tell puts both permanents onto the battlefield at the same time. Before they change zones, both players look at each card.

entries.question: Adriel controls [Wandering Ones] equipped with [Fleetfeather Sandals]. On Nico's turn, they enchant it with [Tightening Coils]. On Adriel's next turn, they activate Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability, targeting Wandering Ones. After that resolves, does it have flying?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes the equip activation gives Fleetfeather Sandals a new timestamp (letting it overwrite Tightening Coils), which contradicts the reference that the equip doesn't change the timestamps so Tightening Coils still applies last.
entries.answer:
Yes — after the equip ability resolves, Wandering Ones has flying (and haste).

Why: Fleetfeather Sandals grants "Equipped creature has flying and haste" and Tightening Coils grants "Enchanted creature gets -6/-0 and loses flying." Both are continuous effects from static abilities that apply in layer 6 (ability-adding and ability-removing effects) [613.1f], and neither depends on the other, so they're ordered by timestamp — the later one wins [613.9].

Initially Tightening Coils had the later timestamp, so Wandering Ones lost flying. But re-activating Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability and attaching it to Wandering Ones again gives that Equipment (and thus the continuous effect from its static ability) a new, later timestamp than Tightening Coils [613.7a], so "Equipped creature has flying" is applied after "loses flying." This matches the card's own ruling: if an effect gives the enchanted creature flying after Tightening Coils became attached, the creature has flying [Tightening Coils ruling #0].

Notes:
- Equip is a sorcery-speed activated ability, so doing this on Adriel's own main phase with an empty stack is legal, and targeting a creature Fleetfeather Sandals is already attached to is fine — the attachment (and timestamp) simply refreshes [604.4].
- The -6/-0 from Tightening Coils is a power/toughness effect in a different layer and is unaffected; Wandering Ones is a -5/1 flier with haste (negative power doesn't kill it).
- Multiple instances of flying would just be redundant [702.9c].
- Player count doesn't matter here; the same result holds in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since only timestamps of Adriel's and Nico's permanents are involved.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Tightening Coils has the most recent timestamp, so its effect is applied last. Activating Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability targeting Wandering Ones doesn't change its timestamp.

entries.question: Addilynn activates the Unearth ability of their [Extractor Demon], returning it to the battlefield. Before their end step, Addilynn casts [Reality Ripple] targeting Extractor Demon. What happens to it?
entries.reason: The candidate hedges and presents conflicting possibilities (even suggesting the demon might permanently avoid exile), whereas the reference gives a definite ruling that it phases out, isn't exiled at the end step, and will phase in at the next untap step and then be subject to the unearth exile replacement thereafter.
entries.answer:
Reality Ripple's phasing doesn't trigger Unearth's exile replacement: Extractor Demon phases out and stays on the battlefield (phased-out permanents don't change zones, they're just "treated as though [they] don't exist" per Reality Ripple's own reminder text), so nothing about phasing out counts as Extractor Demon leaving the battlefield, and Unearth's "if it would leave the battlefield, exile it instead" clause never applies ([702.84a]).

What Unearth still leaves behind is a delayed triggered ability: "Exile it at the beginning of the next end step" ([702.84a], [603.7c]). That delayed ability triggers at the beginning of the end step regardless of Extractor Demon's current characteristics, and it fails to do anything only if Extractor Demon has left the battlefield zone before then ([603.7c]).

Honest limitation: the rules excerpts provided here do not include the phasing rules (rule 702.25/301-style text on how phased-out permanents interact with spells and abilities), so I can't ground from this context whether the end-step exile can reach a permanent that is phased out. Reality Ripple's reminder text — "While it's phased out, it's treated as though it doesn't exist" — points toward the delayed ability not being able to exile it, in which case Extractor Demon simply phases in before Addilynn's next untap step and remains on the battlefield permanently, having dodged Unearth's exile. If instead the delayed ability is treated as able to affect it (since a phased-out permanent is still on the battlefield), Extractor Demon would be exiled at the beginning of the end step.

Timing assumption: I'm reading the question as Reality Ripple resolving before the end step begins, i.e., before the delayed exile trigger goes on the stack. If Reality Ripple were instead cast after that trigger was already on the stack, the trigger would resolve on its own and Extractor Demon's status would be decided by that resolution.

Side note: Extractor Demon's own "whenever another creature leaves the battlefield" ability isn't involved here — phasing out isn't a leaves-the-battlefield event, and that ability only cares about other creatures anyway. In multiplayer, Extractor Demon's trigger may also be limited by range of influence ([801.7a]), but nothing in this scenario depends on that; the phasing/exile answer above is the same with two players or more.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Extractor Demon phases out. When the unearth trigger resolves during Addilynn's end step, it won't be exiled. It will phase back in during Addilynn's next untap step, after which point it will be exiled instead of being put anywhere else if it would leave the battlefield.

entries.question: Avery controls [Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher] and Natalie controls [Verity Circle] and [Koskun Falls]. Avery attacks Natalie with Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher, and then taps it to pay for the cost required by Koskun Falls. Will Natalie's Verity Circle trigger?
entries.reason: The candidate says Verity Circle triggers, but the correct ruling is it does not because tapping Vhal to pay Koskun Falls' attack tax happens as part of declaring it an attacker and so is considered "being declared as an attacker."
entries.answer:
Yes — Natalie's Verity Circle triggers, and Natalie may draw a card.

Why: Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher has vigilance, so declaring it as an attacker doesn't tap it. It becomes tapped later, when Avery activates its mana ability ({T}: add {C} equal to Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher's toughness) to produce mana for Koskun Falls' attack cost. Verity Circle's trigger condition is "whenever a creature an opponent controls becomes tapped, if it isn't being declared as an attacker" — and Verity Circle ruling #2 states plainly that if a creature with vigilance is declared as an attacker and then becomes tapped while attacking, Verity Circle's first ability triggers. Here the tapping is a cost payment via a mana ability, not the tapping that declaring an attacker would cause (compare rule 508.1f, where attacking simply causes creatures to become tapped — that tapping is what the "isn't being declared as an attacker" clause excludes). Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher actually changes from untapped to tapped, which is what Verity Circle ruling #1 requires.

Timing/cost details: Koskun Falls says creatures can't attack Natalie unless their controller pays {2} for each such attacking creature. That cost is determined and locked in during declaration of attackers (508.1h), and because it requires mana Avery gets a chance to activate mana abilities at that point (508.1i, 118.2). Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher is 2/3, so tapping it yields three {C}; {2} is generic mana, so colorless {C} pays it fine (the mana just can't be spent to cast spells from Avery's hand), leaving one {C} floating. If Avery can't pay the {2}, the attack declaration is illegal and is rewound (508.1h, 733 via 508.1f).

Multiplayer note: Koskun Falls only taxes creatures attacking Natalie, its controller, so with more than two players Avery could attack someone else without paying — and then would have no reason to tap Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher, so Verity Circle wouldn't trigger. Also, per Koskun Falls ruling #2, a creature that can't attack Natalie may still attack a planeswalker she controls.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Verity Circle triggers only if the creature being tapped is not being declared as an attacker. Declaring an attacker is a multi-step process, some of which involve determining costs, activating mana abilities, and paying for costs. Therefore, tapping Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher to pay for the cost required by Koskun Falls is part of declaring it as an attacker.

entries.question: Nico controls [Platinum Emperion]. Alexandra attacks with [Hopeful Eidolon], which Nico doesn't block. Does Alexandra gain life?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference: lifelink still causes Alexandra to gain life while Platinum Emperion prevents Nico from losing life, so Alexandra gains life and Nico's total doesn't change.
entries.answer:
Yes — Alexandra gains 1 life, while Nico's life total doesn't change at all.

Hopeful Eidolon is a 1/1 with lifelink, so it deals 1 combat damage to Nico. Damage dealt to a player by a source without infect would normally cause that player to lose that much life [120.3a], but Platinum Emperion says "Your life total can't change," so Nico loses no life. Platinum Emperion doesn't prevent the damage; it only changes the results of that damage [Platinum Emperion ruling #3]. The damage is still dealt, so any of Nico's abilities that trigger on damage being dealt to them would still trigger [Platinum Emperion ruling #4].

Lifelink is a separate result of that same damage: damage dealt by a source with lifelink causes that source's controller to gain that much life, in addition to the damage's other results [702.15b, 120.3f]. That life gain happens to Alexandra, whose life total is unrestricted, so Alexandra gains 1 life. Platinum Emperion ruling #3 states this outcome explicitly: "if a creature with lifelink deals damage to you, you won't lose any life, but its controller will still gain that much life."

Note: if Alexandra had cast Hopeful Eidolon for its bestow cost {3}{W} and attached it to another creature, that creature would get +1/+1 and lifelink, and the same conclusion applies to whatever damage that creature deals to Nico.

This works the same regardless of the number of players at the table — nothing here depends on there being only two players; only Nico's own life total is locked.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Yes. Damage can have 0 or more results. Normally a creature with lifelink dealing damage to a player would have two results:

* Its controller gains that much life.
* The recipient of the damage loses that much life.

Platinum Emperion makes the second result impossible, so only the first occurs.

entries.question: Ari casts a [Hero of Oxid Ridge]. In response, Nixon casts [Hallow], targeting the Hero of Oxid Ridge. When Ari attacks with the Hero of Oxid Ridge that turn, will the damage be prevented?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the opposite conclusion — it says the combat damage won't be prevented, while the reference states that the prevention tied to the spell continues to apply to the permanent and thus the damage is prevented.
entries.answer:
No — the combat damage from Hero of Oxid Ridge will not be prevented.

Hallow says "Prevent all damage target spell would deal this turn." It creates a prevention shield tied to a specific source: the creature spell Hero of Oxid Ridge while it is on the stack. A prevention effect that applies to damage from a source rechecks that source's properties at the time damage would be dealt; if they no longer match, the damage isn't prevented and the shield isn't used up ([609.7b], [615.9], [615.2], [615.1a]). Once Hero of Oxid Ridge resolves, it is no longer a spell on the stack — it's a creature permanent on the battlefield. The combat damage in the combat damage step is dealt by that permanent, not by the spell Hallow targeted, so Hallow prevents nothing (and Nixon gains no life, since he gains life equal to damage prevented, which is 0).

In practice, targeting a creature spell with Hallow accomplishes nothing at all: a creature spell on the stack never deals damage while it is a spell. Hallow is meant for spells that themselves deal damage (burn spells).

Timing note: I'm assuming Nixon cast Hallow while Hero of Oxid Ridge was still on the stack (that's what "in response" and "targeting the Hero" as a spell require) and that it resolved before Hero of Oxid Ridge did. There's no alternative timing that helps — Hallow can only target a spell, so it can't be aimed at the creature permanent later.

This answer is the same whether the game is two players or multiplayer, with one multiplayer caveat: prevention effects only reach sources and recipients within the controller's range of influence ([801.13b]), so in a format with limited range of influence Nixon could only affect things within his range anyway.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Effects that apply to damage from a spell on the stack continue to apply to damage from the permanent that spell becomes.

entries.question: Ariel wants to participate in a sanctioned Magic tournament, but doesn't know where to find one. To which section of the comprehensive rules should they refer?
entries.reason: The candidate correctly identifies rule 100.6b as the section to consult and accurately summarizes its guidance about finding sanctioned tournaments.
entries.answer: Ariel should refer to rule 100.6 — specifically rule 100.6b, which is the rule that tells players where to find tournaments. It states that players can use the Magic Store & Event Locator at Locator.Wizards.com to find tournaments in their area. That same rule (and rule 100.6) also notes that sanctioned tournaments — organized play activities where players compete against other players for prizes — have additional rules covered in the Magic: The Gathering Tournament Rules, found at WPN.Wizards.com/en/rules-documents, which may limit the use of some cards or bar entire older sets. So rule 100.6/100.6b is both the "where do I find a tournament" pointer and the pointer to the extra rules Ariel will be playing under once there.

entries.question: Ariel controls [Mycosynth Lattice]. Nora controls [Kaslem's Strider] enchanted with [Spirit Away]. Ariel casts [Opportunistic Dragon] and takes control of Spirit Away. What will happen after Opportunistic Dragon's ability resolves?

entries.answer:

If Opportunistic Dragon left the battlefield first, the ability does nothing at all — Nora keeps Spirit Away with all abilities intact, and Nora keeps control of Kaslem's Strider anyway [Opportunistic Dragon ruling #3].

entries.question: Atlas attacks with [Pristine Angel], and Nico targets it with [Cephalid Snitch] before blockers. After combat, Atlas casts a spell, untapping Pristine Angel. Once untapped, can Nico target it with [Mob]?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Cephalid Snitch removes only protection from black until end of turn (untapping doesn't restore it), so Mob can legally target Pristine Angel.
entries.answer:
Yes. Nico can target Pristine Angel with Mob. Cephalid Snitch's ability made Pristine Angel lose protection from black until end of turn, and that loss doesn't come back just because Pristine Angel becomes untapped again. Untapping restores the rest of Pristine Angel's protection ability ("As long as this creature is untapped, it has protection from artifacts and from each color"), but the specific protection from black was stripped for the turn by Cephalid Snitch, so a black spell like Mob (a black instant, cost {4}{B}) can legally target and destroy it — Pristine Angel is a 4/4 with no other relevant defense.

Timing assumption: I'm reading it as Cephalid Snitch's ability resolving this turn, and the untap from "Whenever you cast a spell, you may untap this creature" happening later in the same turn. If instead Atlas's spell and the untap happened on a later turn (after the "until end of turn" effect expired), Pristine Angel while untapped would again have protection from each color, and Mob could not target it at all.

Side notes: if Nico were somehow still in combat and tapping attackers/blockers for Mob's convoke, tapping an untapped attacking or blocking creature to convoke doesn't remove it from combat [Mob ruling #4], and Nico may even tap creatures not controlled since the start of their most recent turn [Mob ruling #5]. Likewise, tapping or untapping a creature already declared as an attacker never removes it from combat [506.4b] — so Pristine Angel's untap during combat wouldn't have ended its attack. Convoke doesn't change Mob's mana cost or mana value [Mob ruling #2], and tapping creatures only pays the {4} generic portion or a black creature could pay the {B}.

Nothing here depends on the player count: the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. "Protection from all colors" means the same thing as an individual protection ability for each color, so Pristine Angel will lose protection from black while still having protection from all other colors and from artifacts.

entries.question: Ashley controls a [Gaea's Liege] and 1 [Bayou]. Naomi controls a [Reverence] and 3 Bayous. Can Ashley attack with the Gaea's Liege?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling that Ashley cannot declare Gaea's Liege as an attacker against Naomi because attack legality is checked using its pre-declare power (1) and Reverence prevents creatures with power 2 or less from attacking Naomi.
entries.answer:
No — Ashley can't declare Gaea's Liege as an attacker against Naomi herself.

Why: while Gaea's Liege isn't attacking, its power and toughness each equal the number of Forests Ashley controls. Ashley controls one Bayou, which has the basic land type Forest (Bayou ruling #0/#1: it has basic land types even though it isn't a basic land), so Gaea's Liege is 1/1. Crucially, when checking legality at the moment attackers are declared, you use the "not attacking" power and toughness — it only switches to "Forests defending player controls" after declaration is complete [Gaea's Liege ruling #0]. So Naomi's three Bayous never get counted for this check.

Reverence says "Creatures with power 2 or less can't attack you." That's an attack restriction, and if a restriction is disobeyed the declaration of attackers is illegal [508.1c]. A 1-power Gaea's Liege therefore can't be declared attacking Naomi.

What Ashley can still do:
- Attack a planeswalker Naomi controls, or a battle Naomi protects. Reverence only stops the creature from attacking Naomi, not a planeswalker she controls [Reverence ruling #0]; each attacker independently chooses a defending player, a planeswalker that player controls, or a battle that player protects [802.3a], [310.8b], [508.4c note that only put-onto-the-battlefield-attacking creatures ignore restrictions].
- In a multiplayer game, if Ashley has another opponent in range, Gaea's Liege can attack that opponent (or their planeswalker/battle) freely, since Reverence only protects Naomi [801.3]. Note that if the table uses attack-left/attack-right rules, Ashley may only be allowed to attack one particular neighbor [803.1a]. In a strict two-player game with only Naomi and no planeswalkers or battles, Gaea's Liege simply can't attack.
- If Ashley first raises Gaea's Liege's power above 2 before the declare attackers step — for example by using its own "{T}: Target land becomes a Forest" ability on other lands (though tapping it would also make it ineligible to attack, since chosen attackers must be untapped [508.1a]) — the restriction wouldn't apply. With more Forests under Ashley's control at declaration time, the attack becomes legal.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming the Forest count is as stated at the moment attackers are declared. If Ashley's Forest count changes before that moment, recheck the power then; changes after declaration don't retroactively legalize or illegalize the attack.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Checking to see if any restrictions affect a potentially-attacking creature is done before the creature becomes an "attacking creature".

entries.question: Arjun's [Morality Shift] resolves, in what order do they put cards in their graveyard?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion that Arjun (the owner) chooses the order the cards are placed into his graveyard when Morality Shift resolves.
entries.answer:
Arjun chooses the order himself. When Morality Shift resolves, the cards from Arjun's library are all put into his graveyard at the same time, and because an effect is putting two or more cards into the same graveyard simultaneously, their owner (Arjun) may arrange them in any order he likes [404.3]. This is confirmed directly by the card: "You can choose the order of the cards being placed into the graveyard." [Morality Shift ruling #0]

A few practical notes:
- Once they're in the graveyard, that pile is kept as a single face-up pile and Arjun normally can't rearrange it afterward, though tournament rules may allow reordering [404.2].
- The cards going the other way (his old graveyard) become his new library, and Morality Shift then instructs him to shuffle that library, so their order doesn't matter.
- Morality Shift works even if his graveyard or library was empty beforehand [Morality Shift ruling #1].

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more \u2014 only Arjun, the owner of the cards, makes this ordering choice, so no APNAP ordering among other players is involved.

entries.answer_gold: In the order of Arjun's choice.

entries.question: Ares controls [Gaea's Cradle] and no creatures. Nico controls a [Contamination]. If Ares taps the Gaea's Cradle, what mana is produced, if any?
entries.reason: Both state Gaea's Cradle produces zero mana with no creatures and Contamination has nothing to replace, so no {B} is produced.
entries.answer:
No mana at all. Ares's Gaea's Cradle produces nothing, and Nico's Contamination doesn't turn that into {B}.

Why: Gaea's Cradle's ability is "{T}: Add {G} for each creature you control." With Ares controlling no creatures, the ability resolves and adds zero mana (it is still a mana ability even though it can't produce mana — see [605.2]), and an ability that would add no mana of a defined type simply produces no mana ([106.5]).

Contamination's second ability, "If a land is tapped for mana, it produces {B} instead of any other type and amount," is a replacement effect, not a triggered ability ([Contamination ruling #0]). A replacement effect that applies when a permanent "is tapped for mana" modifies the mana production event while the mana ability is resolving and producing mana ([106.12b]). Here there is no mana production event to modify — Gaea's Cradle produces zero mana — so Contamination has nothing to replace and no {B} appears. Note that Contamination does change the amount as well as the type when it does apply, so with one or more creatures Ares would get exactly {B}, not {G} per creature ([Contamination ruling #2] confirms that effects generating mana based on the type produced are affected in color, while Contamination itself overrides both type and amount for the land's own production).

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players: Contamination affects any land tapped for mana, whoever controls it, so the result is the same at a two-player or multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No mana is produced. Gaea's Cradle is not producing any mana, so Contamination's replacement effect doesn't apply.

entries.question: Aubrey controls a [Necromancy] that was cast during their declare blockers step. During Aubrey's end step, Nikolai activates [Duskmantle Guildmage]'s first ability. Does Aubrey lose 1 life when the Necromancy is sacrificed?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling that Duskmantle Guildmage's delayed trigger will see Necromancy go to Aubrey's graveyard at cleanup and cause Aubrey to lose 1 life.
entries.answer:
Yes — Aubrey loses 1 life when Necromancy is sacrificed (and, in practice, 1 more life when the reanimated creature card is sacrificed too).

Why:

1. Because Aubrey cast Necromancy at a time a sorcery couldn't be cast (their declare blockers step), Necromancy's own text says "the controller of the permanent it becomes sacrifices it at the beginning of the next cleanup step." That sacrifice is mandatory and happens during the cleanup step of that same turn. Sacrificing means Aubrey moves Necromancy from the battlefield directly to its owner's graveyard [701.21a], [Sacrifice].

2. Duskmantle Guildmage's first ability creates a delayed triggered ability that watches for "a card put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere this turn" [Duskmantle Guildmage ruling #0]. Necromancy is a card (not a token), and Aubrey is Nikolai's opponent, so moving Necromancy from the battlefield to Aubrey's graveyard satisfies the condition. Nikolai activated the ability during Aubrey's end step, which is earlier in the same turn as the cleanup step, so the delayed trigger is still live when the sacrifice occurs.

3. Bonus life loss: Necromancy also says "When this enchantment leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it." That leaves-the-battlefield trigger uses "look back in time" rules and will trigger [603.10a]. When that creature card is put into its owner's graveyard, Duskmantle Guildmage's delayed ability triggers again, so Aubrey loses another 1 life (2 total) — unless the reanimated permanent is a token, in which case no life loss for it [Duskmantle Guildmage ruling #1]. Note that if the creature's owner is a different player, the life loss for that card only happens if that owner is also an opponent of Nikolai.

4. If Nikolai had activated the ability more than once, each resolution creates a separate delayed trigger, and each card hitting Aubrey's graveyard triggers all of them [Duskmantle Guildmage ruling #0].

Assumption on timing: I'm reading it as Necromancy having been cast with its own flash-granting ability, which is what causes the cleanup-step sacrifice. If instead some other effect let Aubrey cast it as though it had flash, Necromancy is never sacrificed at cleanup at all and no life is lost [Necromancy ruling #4].

Multiplayer: the answer is the same with more than two players — Duskmantle Guildmage's first ability considers each of Nikolai's opponents, not just one [Duskmantle Guildmage ruling #2], so any opponent's graveyard receiving a card triggers it.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Duskmantle Guildmage creates a delayed triggered ability. The existence of that ability is not a continuous effect, so it still exists during the cleanup step.

entries.question: Alma casts [Virulent Wound], targeting Nico's [Bronze Sable]. In response, Nico casts [Brute Strength] on the Bronze Sable. What happens at the end of the turn?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion: Brute Strength's effect expires, the -1/-1 counter remains so Bronze Sable dies in cleanup, and Virulent Wound's delayed trigger gives Nico a poison counter.
entries.answer:
Bronze Sable survives the combined effects during the turn, but dies during the cleanup step when Brute Strength wears off — and because that still happens "this turn," Virulent Wound's delayed trigger goes off and Nico gets a poison counter.

Step by step:
- Brute Strength resolves first (it was cast in response), giving Bronze Sable +3/+1 and trample until end of turn. Bronze Sable is a base 2/1, so it becomes 5/2.
- Virulent Wound then resolves and puts a -1/-1 counter on Bronze Sable. Counters and the +3/+1 effect are both applied in layer 7 [613.1g], so Bronze Sable is 4/1 — toughness is greater than 0, so it isn't destroyed [704.5f].
- At end of turn, the "until end of turn" effect from Brute Strength expires as the turn's last step ends [500.5a]. The -1/-1 counter stays on Bronze Sable (counters aren't temporary effects), so Bronze Sable is now 2/1 minus 1/-1 = 1/0.
- Toughness 0 or less means Bronze Sable is put into Nico's graveyard as a state-based action; regeneration can't save it [704.5f].
- Virulent Wound's delayed trigger says "When that creature dies this turn, its controller gets a poison counter." Bronze Sable dying during the end-of-turn cleanup is still during that same turn, so the ability triggers and Nico gets a poison counter [Virulent Wound ruling #0 confirms the poison counter only fails to happen if the creature isn't put into a graveyard that turn].

This is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game; only Nico, as Bronze Sable's controller, gets the poison counter.

entries.answer_gold: The effect from Brute Strength wears off, but the -1/-1 counter remains. Bronze Sable dies. The delayed triggered ability created by Virulent Wound is not a continuous effect, so it still exists during the cleanup step, and will trigger due to Bronze Sable dying. Nico gets a poison counter.

entries.question: Angelina controls [Ice Cauldron]. Noel controls [Suppression Field]. Angelina activates Ice Cauldron's first ability with X=1, paying {C}{C}{C}. On Angelina's next turn, they activate Ice Cauldron's second ability. How much mana do they add?

entries.answer:
Angelina adds {C}{C}{C} — three colorless mana — and it can be spent only to cast the card exiled with Ice Cauldron.

Why: Ice Cauldron's first ability ({X}, {T}) is an activated ability that isn't a mana ability, so Suppression Field's "Activated abilities cost {2} more to activate unless they're mana abilities" applies. With X=1, the total activation cost is {1} + {2} = {3} generic mana, which Angelina paid with three colorless mana. Ice Cauldron notes "the type and amount of mana spent to pay this activation cost," and per [Ice Cauldron ruling #8] it counts only the mana actually spent, not the value of X — so the note is {C}{C}{C}, not just {C}.

Ice Cauldron's second ability ({T}, remove a charge counter: add the noted mana) is a mana ability ([Ice Cauldron ruling #0]), so Suppression Field does not tax it ([Suppression Field ruling #0]); Angelina removes the counter and adds exactly the noted {C}{C}{C}. The restriction "Spend this mana only to cast the last card exiled with this artifact" limits use but doesn't change the mana's type ([106.6]), and Angelina may add other mana to help pay the spell's cost ([Ice Cauldron ruling #5]).

This works the same regardless of the number of players; Suppression Field affects activated abilities of all players, so Noel controlling it still taxes Angelina.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Just {C}. The activation cost of Ice Cauldron's first ability is "{X}, {T}". The additional cost imposed by Suppression Field is not part of the activation cost, and the mana spent on it isn't noted when the ability resolves.

entries.question: Ariel activates [Warped Landscape]. Before that resolves Noe casts [Aven Mindcensor]. When Ariel is resolving Warped Landscape's ability, they find [Panglacial Wurm] in the top four cards of their library. Can they cast it?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Aven Mindcensor only restricts the search to the top four (doesn't eliminate the search), so Panglacial Wurm found there can be cast.
entries.answer:
Yes — Ariel can cast Panglacial Wurm from their library.

Why: Panglacial Wurm says "While you're searching your library, you may cast this card from your library." Aven Mindcensor doesn't stop the search from being a search; it only shrinks it to the top four cards. Replacing a search of a zone with a search of a portion of that zone still counts as searching that zone, and other instructions referring to the search still apply [701.23f], and Aven Mindcensor's own ruling confirms that searching the top four counts as searching that library [Aven Mindcensor ruling #0]. Since Panglacial Wurm is among the top four, Ariel is allowed to see it and may cast it from the library.

Timing and mechanics:
- Ariel must cast Panglacial Wurm before finding a card with Warped Landscape's search — once the basic land is found, the window closes [Panglacial Wurm ruling #1].
- Casting follows all normal rules except timing and zone: it goes on the stack, Ariel pays {5}{G}{G} plus any additional costs, and mana abilities may be activated during the casting even though this happens mid-resolution of Warped Landscape's ability [Panglacial Wurm ruling #0].
- After casting, Ariel resumes the search where they left off; when Warped Landscape's ability finishes resolving (search the restricted top four for a basic land, put it onto the battlefield tapped, then shuffle the entire library [Aven Mindcensor ruling #1]), the active player gets priority with Panglacial Wurm on the stack and cast-triggers go on the stack then [Panglacial Wurm ruling #3].
- Panglacial Wurm, having been cast, can't also be found by the search [Panglacial Wurm ruling #4]. If Ariel has the mana, multiple Panglacial Wurms could be cast in one search [Panglacial Wurm ruling #5].
- Keep the library in its existing order until the shuffle [Panglacial Wurm ruling #2].

Note the flip side: if Panglacial Wurm were the fifth card or deeper, Aven Mindcensor would prevent Ariel from looking at it at all, so it couldn't be identified or cast that way [Aven Mindcensor ruling #2]. Here it's in the top four, so it's fine.

Multiplayer: no difference. Aven Mindcensor applies to each of Noe's opponents who would search a library, so Ariel is affected identically whether the game has two players or more.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Aven Mindcensor's ability is a replacement effect that replaces searching a library with searching only the top four cards of that library. However for the purposes of Panglacial Wurm's effect, it still qualifies as "searching a library".

entries.question: Addison has cast a sideboard card from [Glittering Wish], which is now in their graveyard. Addison then restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. What happens?
entries.reason: Both conclude the card fetched from the sideboard by Glittering Wish becomes part of Addison’s deck for the restarted game (the candidate also notes Glittering Wish itself joins the new-game library, consistent with the full explanation).
entries.answer:
The card Addison fetched with Glittering Wish stays in the game and becomes part of Addison's new-game deck, and Glittering Wish itself (which exiled itself on resolution) also goes into that deck.

Details:

1. Glittering Wish lets Addison reveal a multicolored card they own from outside the game (in a tournament, from their sideboard) and put it into their hand; Glittering Wish is then exiled [Glittering Wish ruling #0]. "Outside the game" is not a zone 	here outside any of the game's zones, and sideboard cards are outside the game [400.11a].
2. When Karn Liberated's −14 ability restarts the game, that game immediately ends with no winner, loser, or drawer, and all players still in it immediately begin a new game following the normal starting-the-game procedure [727.1], [104.6], [Karn Liberated ruling #12], [Karn Liberated ruling #9].
3. Every Magic card involved in the ended game is involved in the new game, even cards that weren't originally part of it — and ownership doesn't change. So the sideboard card Addison brought in with Glittering Wish (wherever it ended up — battlefield, graveyard, or exile) is shuffled into Addison's library for the new game, exactly like the Living Wish example [727.2]. Glittering Wish itself, sitting in exile (or the graveyard as you described), likewise becomes part of Addison's new-game library.
4. The only exceptions are cards an effect exempts from the restart procedure [727.5] — here, the non-Aura permanent cards that Karn Liberated's own first or second ability exiled remain in exile and are then put onto the battlefield under Addison's control after the pregame procedure, just before the first turn [Karn Liberated ruling #6], [Karn Liberated ruling #4], [727.4]. If the wished-for card happened to be a non-Aura permanent card that Karn Liberated had exiled with +4 or −3, it stays in exile and enters the battlefield under Addison's control instead of going to the library.
5. Addison cannot use the restart as an opportunity to reorganize: players can't move cards between deck and sideboard before the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #5]. Set-aside sideboards are not part of the starting deck [103.2a], but a wished card that entered the game is no longer in the sideboard — it's a game card and joins the library.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Glittering Wish had fully resolved (and the fetched card was cast) before Karn Liberated's −14 resolved. If instead Karn Liberated's ability resolved while Glittering Wish were still on the stack, the game would still restart and Glittering Wish would end up in Addison's library the same way, just without a fetched card having entered the game.

Two players vs. more: the answer is the same either way, except that in a multiplayer game any player who had already left before the restart isn't in the new game, and their cards aren't either [Karn Liberated ruling #11], [Karn Liberated ruling #3]. Addison, as the controller of the restarting ability, is the starting player in the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #9].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The sideboard card is shuffled into Addison's library for the restarted game.

entries.question: Alvin controls [Mycosynth Lattice], a [Dance of the Dead] attached to a [Streetbreaker Wurm] that it returned to the battlefield, and a [Mizzium Transreliquat] that is currently a copy of [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces] due to its second ability. Alvin casts [Eureka], choosing to put [March of the Machines] onto the battlefield, then putting [Copy Artifact] onto the battlefield, which copies the Mizzium Transreliquat and then copies the Dance of the Dead with its new copy ability. (The one from Sakashima of a Thousand Faces.) They choose for it to enchant a [Viashino Warrior] in their graveyard. As Eureka continues resolving, they put [Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked] onto the battlefield and sacrifice March of the Machines. After Copy Artifact's trigger resolves and returns the Viashino Warrior to the battlefield, Alvin activates the ability of the Copy Artifact to turn it into a copy of Streetbreaker Wurm. What happens?
entries.reason: Both say the Copy Artifact stops being the Aura and becomes a Streetbreaker Wurm copy (keeping the copy ability), unattaches from the Viashino, and because it didn't leave the battlefield no Dance of the Dead leaves-the-battlefield trigger occurs so the Viashino stays (a sacrifice would only be required if the Copy Artifact later left the battlefield).
entries.answer:
Bottom line: the Copy Artifact permanent becomes a colorless 6/4 Wurm named Streetbreaker Wurm (an artifact, because of Mycosynth Lattice) that still has the {1}{U}{R} copy ability, it stops being an Aura and stops enchanting the returned Viashino Warrior — and because it never left the battlefield, Dance of the Dead's leaves-the-battlefield trigger never triggers, so Alvin simply keeps the Viashino Warrior with no sacrifice.

Step by step:

1. Copy Artifact entering as a copy of Mizzium Transreliquat: Mizzium Transreliquat's second ability had permanently made it a copy of Sakashima of a Thousand Faces with that {1}{U}{R} ability, and copy effects already applying to a permanent are part of its copiable values [707.2] [707.3] [Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #3]. So Copy Artifact enters as Sakashima of a Thousand Faces plus the {1}{U}{R} "becomes a copy of target artifact, except it has this ability" ability, and, per Copy Artifact's own exception, it is an enchantment in addition to its other types [707.9b] [Copy Artifact ruling #2].

2. Copying Dance of the Dead: Dance of the Dead is an artifact because of Mycosynth Lattice, so it is a legal target for the {1}{U}{R} ability [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #1]. The new copy overwrites what the permanent was copying and it keeps that ability [Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #0] [Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #2]. Its Dance of the Dead text refers only to itself, not to Alvin's original Dance of the Dead [201.5b] — so its enters trigger set up its own "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura," returned Viashino Warrior tapped under Alvin's control, and attached to it [Dance of the Dead ruling #1].

3. Why March of the Machines didn't kill everything: with Mycosynth Lattice plus March of the Machines, every noncreature artifact — including the Auras — would become an artifact creature, and an Aura that's a creature unattaches and is then put into the graveyard as state-based actions [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3] [March of the Machines ruling #1]. But state-based actions are only checked when a player would receive priority, and Eureka put Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked onto the battlefield and sacrificed March of the Machines during that same resolution [Eureka ruling #3]. By the time anyone got priority, March of the Machines was gone, so no Aura was ever unattached or destroyed.

4. The final activation: the {1}{U}{R} ability targets Streetbreaker Wurm, legal because Mycosynth Lattice makes it an artifact. Note the cost is {1}{U}{R}, i.e. one generic plus one blue plus one red — Mycosynth Lattice lets Alvin spend mana as though it were any color, so any three mana works (restrictions on the mana still apply) [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #0]. The permanent's copiable values become those of Streetbreaker Wurm, except it keeps that ability; it does not copy the +1/+1 or the no-untap effect and it is no longer an Aura at all [707.2] [707.3]. It's colorless because of Mycosynth Lattice [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #2].

5. The payoff: becoming a copy of something else while remaining on the battlefield does not trigger leaves-the-battlefield abilities [707.4], so "When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it" never triggers. Viashino Warrior stays on the battlefield under Alvin's control as a plain 4/2 (colorless artifact Lizard Warrior via Mycosynth Lattice), it loses the +1/+1, and it will untap normally in Alvin's untap step. The new Streetbreaker Wurm copy has summoning sickness (Alvin hasn't controlled it since their turn began), so it can't attack or use {T} abilities this turn [March of the Machines ruling #4]. Alvin's original Dance of the Dead on the original Streetbreaker Wurm is untouched.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming both copy effects were applied as the Copy Artifact entered the battlefield (as your description states), which is why the Dance of the Dead enters trigger occurred and returned Viashino Warrior. If instead the permanent was already on the battlefield and only then activated the ability to become Dance of the Dead, rule 707.4 means no enters-the-battlefield ability would trigger and Viashino Warrior would never have been returned at all.

entries.question: Aspen controls a [Blood Tyrant] that they took control of from Briella using [Malevolent Whispers]. Aspen has 1 life. Cason casts [Volt Charge] targeting Aspen. After it resolves and Aspen loses the game, will Blood Tyrant get the +1/+1 counters?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes the trigger occurs and can place counters (at least in multiplayer), whereas the reference concludes the trigger never gets placed on the stack when Aspen leaves the game so no counters are added.
entries.answer:
Direct answer: Yes — Blood Tyrant's third ability does trigger when Aspen loses the game, but whether the five +1/+1 counters actually get placed depends on the number of players.

What happens step by step:
1. Volt Charge deals 3 damage to Aspen. Damage is processed into its result — loss of 3 life — so Aspen goes from 1 life to −2 [120.4c].
2. A player at 0 or less life loses the game as a state-based action [119.6].
3. Blood Tyrant's "Whenever a player loses the game" ability triggers regardless of how the player lost, including a state-based action from life total [603.9], [Blood Tyrant ruling #1]. Abilities that trigger on a player losing the game "look back in time," meaning the game uses the existence of the ability and the appearance of objects immediately before the event [603.10f]. So the fact that Aspen (and Aspen's control of Blood Tyrant via Malevolent Whispers) is gone the instant afterward does not stop the trigger.

Two-player game (Aspen and Cason only, with Briella not in it): if Aspen's loss ends the game, nothing further matters — the counters are irrelevant.

Multiplayer game (Aspen, Briella, Cason all present): the game continues after Aspen leaves [800.4a]. When Aspen leaves, all effects giving Aspen control of objects end, so Malevolent Whispers' control effect ends and Blood Tyrant reverts to Briella's control (Blood Tyrant is Briella's card, so it is not exiled or removed with Aspen) [800.4a]. The trigger from Aspen's loss still occurred by looking back in time [603.10f], and when it resolves it puts five +1/+1 counters on Blood Tyrant — which is now on the battlefield under Briella's control. Note that 800.4a also says objects on the stack that are not represented by cards and are controlled by the departing player cease to exist; the rules provided here don't spell out who controls this particular trigger given it triggered at the exact moment Aspen left, so if your table rules that the trigger was Aspen's and on the stack, it would cease to exist and no counters would be added.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Volt Charge finished resolving (damage dealt, then proliferate) and the state-based action for Aspen's life total was checked immediately after. If instead Aspen had somehow already left the game before Volt Charge resolved, there would be no "loses the game" event from this spell at all and no trigger.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. As Aspen loses the game, the effect granting them control of Blood Tyrant ends, and it returns to Briella. "Loses the game" triggers use the game state immediately before they triggered to determine how that trigger is handled. Since Aspen controlled Blood Tyrant right before losing the game, the trigger would be placed onto the stack under their control. However Aspen is no longer in the game when the trigger would be placed onto the stack, so it never is.

entries.question: Aspen, Brycen, and Collins begin a multiplayer game. In Aspen's upkeep, they use [Leyline of Anticipation], several [Simian Spirit Guide]s and [Desperate Ritual]s, and [Goblin Charbelcher] to kill Brycen. Does Aspen draw a card for the turn?
entries.reason: Both conclude Aspen still draws because the game is multiplayer so the draw step occurs even after Brycen is killed, matching the reference ruling.
entries.answer:
Yes — Aspen draws a card in their draw step.

Why: This is a multiplayer game (Aspen, Brycen, Collins), and in multiplayer games no player skips the draw step of their first turn, including the starting player [103.8c]. Immediately after the draw step begins, the active player (Aspen) draws a card as a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack [703.4d, 504.1].

Nothing about killing Brycen changes that. Brycen loses the game and therefore leaves the game [104.5], but a multiplayer game continues after one or more players have left [800.4k], and Collins is still an opponent, so Aspen doesn't win the game — a player only wins that way when all of their opponents have left [104.2a]. Note also that if a triggered ability that watches for a player losing the game exists, it triggers on Brycen leaving [603.9].

On the setup: Leyline of Anticipation may start on the battlefield from Aspen's opening hand, and such actions are taken before the first turn begins [Leyline of Anticipation ruling #0]; it then lets Aspen cast spells as though they had flash, which matters because Desperate Ritual is not a mana ability — it's a spell that uses the stack and can be responded to [Desperate Ritual ruling #4]. Simian Spirit Guide's exile ability is a mana ability and can be used any time Aspen could pay mana. Goblin Charbelcher's target must be chosen as the ability is activated, before any cards are revealed [Goblin Charbelcher ruling #1], so Brycen had to be chosen as the target up front.

Timing note: I'm assuming all of this happens during Aspen's upkeep step, i.e. before the draw step begins, as stated. Since the draw is a turn-based action at the start of Aspen's draw step, Aspen still draws regardless. In a two-player game, killing the only opponent during upkeep would instead end the game immediately [104.2a], so no draw would occur.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. The game began with more than 2 players, so it is a multiplayer game, regardless of the current number of players remaining.. Aspen will draw a card during their draw step.

entries.question: Addison, Brixton, and Collins started playing a multiplayer game. Collins lost the game, and then Addison restarted the game with [Karn Liberated]. Will Addison draw a card on the first turn of the restarted game?

Yes — Addison draws a card during the draw step of the first turn of the restarted game.

Why: Karn Liberated's −14 restarts the game, and the player who controlled the ability that restarted it is the starting player in the new game, so Addison goes first [727.1a] [Karn Liberated ruling #9]. Because Collins had already lost and left the game before the restart, Collins isn't involved in the new game, so only Addison and Brixton play it [Karn Liberated ruling #11] [727.2 covers cards; 800.4k].

The draw is a turn-based action taken immediately as the draw step begins and doesn't use the stack [703.4d] [504.1]. Only in a genuine two-player game does the player who plays first skip that draw [103.8a] — so if instead Addison and Brixton had begun the match as a two-player game, Addison would skip the first draw step.

Two related timing notes: Karn Liberated's ability finishes resolving (putting the exiled non-Aura permanent cards onto the battlefield under Addison's control) just before the first turn's untap step, and any resulting triggers go on the stack in the first upkeep step [727.4] [Karn Liberated ruling #4]. Also, since everyone draws seven, any player with fewer than seven cards in their library loses when state-based actions are checked in that first upkeep step [727.3].

entries.question: Aniyah casts [Martyrdom], targeting their [Douser of Lights]. After it resolves, Nico takes control of Douser of Lights with [Act of Aggression]. Can Nico activate the ability it gained from Martyrdom?
entries.reason: The candidate's conclusion contradicts the correct ruling — "you" in Martyrdom's granted activation instruction refers to the permanent's current controller, so Nico (the current controller) could activate the ability.
entries.answer:
No. Nico can't activate the ability. Martyrdom's granted ability comes with the instruction "Only you may activate this ability," where "you" is Aniyah, the controller of Martyrdom. Under rule 113.10a, when an effect adds an activated ability it may include activation instructions, and those instructions become part of the ability that's added to the object. So the restriction travels with the ability on Douser of Lights.

Rule 602.5b confirms that a restriction on an activated ability's use continues to apply to that object even if its controller changes. Act of Aggression gives Nico control of Douser of Lights until end of turn (untapped, with haste), but it doesn't rewrite who "you" is in the ability Martyrdom granted — that still refers to Aniyah. A player can't begin to activate an ability that's prohibited from being activated (602.5), and Martyrdom's own text overrides the general expectation that a permanent's controller is the one who activates its abilities.

Practically: Aniyah is the only player who may activate the "{0}: The next 1 damage..." ability, even while Nico controls Douser of Lights, and the redirected damage would still be dealt to Douser of Lights. If Douser of Lights leaves the battlefield or stops being a creature before the damage is redirected, the damage stays where it was (Martyrdom rulings #1 and #2).

This works the same whether the game has two players or more; Act of Aggression just needs the creature to be controlled by an opponent of its caster.

entries.answer_gold: Yes. "Only you may activate this ability." is an activation instruction for the ability, and it is part of the ability gained by the Douser of Lights. "You" therefore refers to the permanent's current controller.

entries.question: Ashley has restarted the game with a [Karn Liberated] that exiled an [Ajani's Chosen]. Ashley chooses to begin the restarted game with a [Leyline of Anticipation] on the battlefield. Does Ajani's Chosen trigger?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Ajani's Chosen does not trigger because Leyline of Anticipation is put onto the battlefield during the pregame procedure before Ajani's Chosen is returned to the battlefield by Karn's restart.
entries.answer:
No — Ajani's Chosen does not trigger. Leyline of Anticipation enters the battlefield during the pregame procedure, as part of the opening-hand actions taken after mulligans are complete ([103.6a], [Leyline of Anticipation ruling #0], [Karn Liberated ruling #9]). Karn Liberated's restart effect only finishes resolving after that pregame procedure is complete and just before the first turn's untap step, and that is when the exiled Ajani's Chosen is put onto the battlefield under Ashley's control ([727.4], [Karn Liberated ruling #4]).

So at the moment Leyline of Anticipation enters, Ajani's Chosen isn't on the battlefield yet and has no ability in effect to trigger. Ajani's Chosen's ability is a triggered ability that only triggers on an enchantment entering while Ajani's Chosen is already on the battlefield; there's no "looking back in time" for enters-the-battlefield triggers ([603.10a] lists the narrow exceptions, which don't include this), and Ajani's Chosen's own ability requires the enchantment to enter ([Ajani's Chosen ruling #3]).

Ashley's Ajani's Chosen will, however, have been on the battlefield continuously since the start of Ashley's first turn, so it can attack that turn ([Karn Liberated ruling #2]), and it will trigger on any later enchantment Ashley controls entering. If instead some other trigger did happen as Karn Liberated's ability finished resolving, it would go on the stack at the beginning of the first upkeep step ([727.4], [Karn Liberated ruling #4]).

This answer is the same whether the table is two players or more; the only multiplayer wrinkle provided is that any player who had already left before the restart isn't in the new game ([727.7], [Karn Liberated ruling #11]).

entries.answer_gold: No. Leyline of Anticipation is put onto the battlefield before the Ajani's Chosen is.

entries.question: Nehemiah controls a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 2 +1/+1 counters on it. Ari casts [Bishop of Binding], exiling the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave. When Ari attacks with Bishop of Binding on their next turn, what will X equal in Bishop of Binding's triggered ability?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that counters remain on Skullbriar in exile, making it a 3/3, and that Bishop of Binding's trigger sets X to that power (3) when it resolves.
entries.answer:
X will be 3.

Skullbriar, the Walking Grave is printed 1/1 and had 2 +1/+1 counters on it. Normally, [Bishop of Binding ruling #1] says any counters on the creature exiled by Bishop of Binding cease to exist — but Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own text reads "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." Exile is not a hand or library, so the counters stay, and that specific card text overrides the general behavior described in the ruling.

Because +1/+1 counters modify power and toughness even in zones other than the battlefield ([122.1a], and confirmed by [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2], which notes a Skullbriar in the command zone with a +1/+1 counter is 2/2), the exiled Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card in exile is 3/3. Skullbriar, the Walking Grave also had the relevant ability in the zone it left (the battlefield), which is what [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1] requires.

Bishop of Binding's attack trigger sets X to the power of the exiled card, and that value is determined only as the ability resolves ([Bishop of Binding ruling #5]). So as it resolves on Ari's next turn, X = 3, and the target Vampire gets +3/+3 until end of turn. Caveats: if Bishop of Binding leaves the battlefield before the attack trigger resolves, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave returns and there is no exiled card, making X = 0 ([Bishop of Binding ruling #0]). If Skullbriar, the Walking Grave gained or lost counters in the meantime, use its power at resolution.

Nothing here depends on player count — the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since Bishop of Binding just targets a creature an opponent controls.
